entries.defect: The struct name index was keyed only by name, so same-named structs from different modules collided and lookups could return another module's struct.

findings.summary: The fallback for a `GenericInstance` with empty type args now looks up the plain struct by name only and no longer checks `module_source`, so it can return a struct with the same name from a different module.
findings.detail: The old loop matched only if both `struct_name == &name` and `struct_source == &module_source`. `find_struct_by_name(&name)` drops the module check. If a user module and a stdlib or dependency module both define a struct with the same name (for example `Error` or `Node`), substituting `Container<T>`-style self references inside a generic method can resolve to the other module's struct. The result is wrong field layouts or types in generated code, or type mismatches.

findings.summary: `struct_name_index` keeps the last struct interned under a name, while the replaced linear scans returned the first one, so name lookups now pick a different `TypeId` when several Struct entries share a name.
findings.detail: `intern` and `retain` call `struct_name_index.insert(name, id)` without a check, so every later Struct with the same name (another module, or a different `is_monomorphized`/`base_name`) overwrites the earlier entry. All three call sites in `monomorphize.rs` used to return the first match in insertion order. Programs where two Struct types share a name now resolve to a different `TypeId` than before.

findings.summary: The new global `known_type_names_cache` leaves out names brought in by import aliases (`use { Foo as Bar }`), so `is_known_type_name("Bar")` now returns false.
findings.detail: The removed `rebuild_known_type_names_cache` also took keys from the per-module flat maps (`struct_fields`, `newtypes`, `variant_cases`, ...). `build_module_map` fills those maps with aliased local names. The global cache only collects the original declared names from the `all_*` maps. An aliased type is therefore treated as a free type parameter in `impl` handling (`resolver.rs` ~401/448, `module.rs` ~335/373, `method_lookup.rs` 113/118/1478/1610). For example, `impl Trait for Array<Bar>` is treated as a blanket impl over a type variable, so trait impls get registered for the wrong types. Also, `Bar::missing()` no longer reports `UnknownFunction` (`call.rs` 463), so a diagnostic is missed.

findings.summary: `replace_type` does not update `struct_name_index`, so the index goes stale after the boxing pass rewrites a type into a Struct.
findings.detail: `replace_type` (used by `lower/boxing.rs` to rewrite `Ref(primitive)` into `Struct(Box<T>)`) writes `self.types` directly without touching `struct_name_index`. Afterwards `find_struct_by_name` misses structs that a scan of `types` would find, and it may return an id whose entry is no longer a Struct with that name. Unlike the old `iter_type_ids` scan, the index does not see replaced entries, so any later name lookup can give a wrong result.

grade.reason: Finding 0 identifies that find_struct_by_name looks up by name only, dropping the module_source check, so it can return a same-named struct from another module, which is exactly the known defect.

findings.summary: The fallback lookup for a GenericInstance with no type args now matches a struct by name only. It drops the `module_source` check, so a same-named struct from another module can be returned.
findings.detail: The old fallback matched both `struct_name == &name` and `struct_source == &module_source`. The new `type_table.find_struct_by_name(&name)` ignores the module. `TypeTable::struct_name_index` keeps one TypeId per name, and the last struct interned wins. `ResolvedType::Struct` includes `module_source`, so two modules that each define a struct with the same name (for example a user `Node` or `Error` and another module's) get two separate TypeIds. Substitution can then rewrite the type to the other module's struct, which gives wrong field layouts or methods, or type errors in codegen. The other two rewritten lookups (mangled names) also change from first-match to last-match when names collide.

findings.summary: Each module's `known_type_names_cache` is now one global set built only from the declared names in the `all_*` maps. Import aliases (`use { Foo as Bar }`) are no longer recognised as known type names.
findings.detail: The removed `rebuild_known_type_names_cache` also took keys from the module's own flat maps (`struct_fields`, `variant_cases`, `newtypes`, etc.). `build_module_map` adds the aliased local name to those maps (`result.insert(local_name.clone(), value)`), so `Bar` used to count as known. The global set only has original declaration names, so `is_known_type_name("Bar")` is now false. This changes behaviour wherever the check is used. `impl Trait for Bar` is treated as a blanket impl over a free type parameter (method_lookup.rs:1478, 1610), so impls can match any receiver. `impl<Bar, T>` / `Trait<Bar>` arguments are registered as type parameters instead of concrete types (module.rs:335/373, resolver.rs:401/448). Calling a missing static method such as `Bar::nope()` no longer reports UnknownFunction (call.rs:463).

grade.reason: Finding 0 identifies that struct_name_index/find_struct_by_name is keyed only by name, dropping module_source, so same-named structs from different modules collide — exactly the fixed defect.

findings.summary: The plain-struct fallback for an empty-args GenericInstance now matches on name alone and ignores `module_source`, so it can return a struct from a different module.
findings.detail: Struct identity includes `module_source`: `make_struct` interns `(name, module_source, ...)`, and `find_struct_type` keys on both. The old fallback loop required both `struct_name == &name` and `struct_source == &module_source`. The new `find_struct_by_name(&name)` reads a single index where each insert overwrites the last, so it keeps only the most recently interned struct with that name. Suppose two modules each define a struct with the same name, for example a user `Node` and a stdlib `Node`, or two packages' `Error`. Then substituting a `GenericInstance` with empty args (as happens inside generic methods) can resolve to the other module's struct. That produces wrong types in monomorphized code, with wrong field layouts or failing lookups.

findings.summary: `struct_name_index` overwrites on each insert (last wins), while the loops it replaces returned the first match, so the mangled-name lookups now give different TypeIds when names collide.
findings.detail: `intern()` runs `struct_name_index.insert(name.clone(), id)` for every new Struct. Struct types are interned per `(name, module_source, is_monomorphized, base_name)`, so several TypeIds can share one name, for example `Box<i32>` monomorphized from same-named generics in different modules, or a plain struct whose name equals a mangled name. The removed code in `monomorphize.rs` walked `iter_type_ids()` in insertion order and returned the first match. The index returns the last. `retain()` also rebuilds the index with last-wins. `substitute_type` can therefore pick a different struct than before whenever two struct types share a name.

findings.summary: The precomputed global `known_type_names_cache` drops the per-module names the old `rebuild_known_type_names_cache` included, such as import aliases (`use { Foo as Bar }`), so aliased types are not recognised as known type names.
findings.detail: The old cache added keys from the per-module flat maps (`struct_fields`, `variant_cases`, `enum_cases`, `flags_cases`, `newtypes`, `generic_newtype_defs`). `build_module_map` fills those maps with alias names under `local_name`. The new global set holds only the original names from the `all_*` maps, so an alias like `Bar` is missing. As a result, `Bar::unknown()` no longer gets the UnknownFunction diagnostic at call.rs:463. Instead it falls through to the effect/module-namespace path and is treated as a call on `ModuleSource::Local { path: "Bar" }`, so the user's error goes unreported. The method_lookup.rs and module.rs checks that use `is_known_type_name` to tell type parameters from concrete types (for example `is_blanket_type_param`) also misclassify the aliased name as a type parameter, which can choose the wrong blanket impl.

grade.reason: Finding 0 identifies that find_struct_by_name keys only on name, ignoring module_source, so same-named structs from different modules collide and lookups can return the wrong module's struct; this is exactly the defect the fix addresses.

entries.defect: compile_one used a silent host and threw away the compiler's diagnostics, both through `map_err(|_| "compilation failed")` and by silently producing empty output when the dump returned None, so fixture-generation failures were reported with no reason.

findings.summary: If every dump worker panics, for example from a compiler panic or stack overflow on enough fixtures, the reader thread blocks forever and the tool hangs instead of failing.
findings.detail: Each worker gets a clone of the `Arc<Mutex<Receiver>>`, but `run_pipeline` also keeps the original `read_rx` Arc until it returns. When all workers have died, nothing reads from the bounded `sync_channel(2 * num_workers)`, yet the receiver is never dropped. The reader thread therefore stays blocked in `read_tx.send(item)` and never gets the error that would end its loop. The writer loop ends because every `write_tx` is gone, and then `reader.join()` waits forever, so the 'dump worker panicked' failure is never reported. The old code turned a crashed thread into an error message and panicked.

findings.summary: Using `--skip-empty` for all phases makes real compile failures on format fixtures pass silently: the golden file is deleted and the script still reports success.
findings.detail: In `run_pipeline`, `skip_empty` covers both empty output and the `Err(e)` branch, so a failed compile is logged as 'Skipped' and counted as a skip. The old script stopped with exit 1 ('WARNING: failed to generate ...') whenever a dump failed. It only skipped files that are explicitly marked `#![no_prelude]`. Now, if a compiler change breaks `all.dirty.wado` or `mess.dirty.wado`, the script deletes their `.tir/.lower/.wir/.wat` golden files and prints 'Golden format fixtures updated.' The regression is not reported.

findings.summary: The `tir` phase now writes only the entry-point module, so `.tir.wado` and `.optimize.wado` golden files no longer show the TIR of the other modules.
findings.detail: Before, these files came from `wado dump --tir` and contained every module (`core:allocator`, `core:builtin`, `core:internal`, `core:prelude/string.wado`, and so on). `compile_one`'s `Phase::Tir` stops after the first `is_entry_point()` module, as the regenerated golden diffs show: all non-entry module content is gone. The phase golden files exist to track compiler output across phases, so changes in optimized stdlib or allocator code no longer appear in them. The header also hardcodes '-O2' whatever opt level was requested.

grade.reason: No finding covers compile_one discarding diagnostics from the silent host or producing empty output with no reason; the findings are about a worker-panic hang, skip-empty masking failures, and TIR covering only the entry module.

findings.summary: Running every phase with `--skip-empty` hides real compile failures: the fixture is skipped silently and its existing golden file is deleted.
findings.detail: In `pipeline.rs`, when `skip_empty` is set, the `Err(e)` branch (a compile failure or a WAT printing error) only prints "Skipped …", counts the file as skipped and returns success. It also calls `fs::remove_file` on the output first. The old script exited with an error whenever a dump failed. Now, if a regression makes `all.dirty.wado` or `mess.dirty.wado` stop compiling, the script prints "Golden format fixtures updated." and exits 0 after deleting the `.tir/.lower/.optimize/.wir/.wat` goldens. The flag was meant only to cover `no_prelude` files that produce empty output, but it covers every error.

findings.summary: The worker count is now the full CPU count, removing the old cap at half the CPUs that existed to prevent SIGSEGV and memory pressure.
findings.detail: The removed `run_bulk` capped concurrency at `available_parallelism()/2` (minimum 2). Its comments say each compilation uses about 16 MB of stack plus a lot of heap, and that the cap was needed to avoid SIGSEGV under memory pressure. `run_pipeline` starts `available_parallelism()` workers, each with a 16 MB stack, an 8 MB alternate signal stack and a full compiler pipeline. That doubles peak memory, so `mise run update-golden-fixtures` is more likely to be OOM-killed or crash on machines with many cores and little memory, which is the failure the cap was added for.

findings.summary: The new host is always silent, so a failed fixture reports only "compilation failed" and none of the compiler's diagnostics.
findings.detail: `FilesystemCompilerHost::silent` sets `print_diagnostics: false` and `LogLevel::Off`, and the pipeline throws away the error detail with `map_err(|_| "compilation failed")`. The old script called `wado dump`/`compile`, whose host printed the error diagnostics. The new tool never shows the reason, so when golden generation panics the user cannot see which error caused it.

findings.summary: The `.tir.wado` and `.optimize.wado` format goldens now contain only the entry module, so all other modules' TIR silently drops out of these goldens.
findings.detail: `Phase::Tir` writes only the module where `is_entry_point()` is true and adds a hardcoded "Optimized TIR with -O2" header. The old `wado dump --tir` printed every module (allocator, builtin, prelude, and so on), as the deleted lines in the regenerated goldens show. The `.tir.wado` phase is also run without `-O`, so it falls back to O2 and gives the same file as `.optimize.wado`; the regenerated goldens are byte-identical. As a result, changes to non-entry modules' TIR no longer appear in these goldens.

grade.reason: Finding 2 identifies the silent host and the `map_err(|_| "compilation failed")` that discard the compiler diagnostics, which is the root cause the fix addresses.

findings.summary: Passing `--skip-empty` to every phase means a fixture that fails to compile no longer fails the script: its existing golden file is deleted and the script still exits successfully.
findings.detail: In `run_pipeline`, the `Err(e)` branch also honours `skip_empty`. It deletes the output file, prints "Skipped ..." and counts the file as skipped. The flag was meant only for no_prelude files that produce empty output, but it now also hides real compile errors and WAT printing errors for `all`, `mess`, `ops.*` and the rest. The old `run_dump` stopped with `exit 1` and kept the existing target file on failure. Now a compiler regression quietly removes golden outputs and the script reports success.

findings.summary: If every dump worker thread panics, `reader.join()` waits forever, so the tool hangs instead of reporting the panic.
findings.detail: The main thread keeps its own `Arc` of the shared `read_rx` until the function returns, so the channel receiver is never dropped even when all workers are gone. Workers die if `compile_one` panics on several fixtures, one per worker. Once that happens and the bounded `read_tx` buffer (2*num_workers) is full, the reader thread blocks in `send` forever. The writer loop ends because all `write_tx` clones are dropped. Then `reader.join()` runs before the worker joins and never returns, so the panic is never reported.

findings.summary: The `tir` phase writes only the entry-point module, so the regenerated `*.tir.wado` / `*.optimize.wado` format goldens lose the TIR of every other module.
findings.detail: The script used to run `wado dump --tir`, which printed every module (core:allocator, core:builtin, core:internal, String and so on). The new `Phase::Tir` stops after the first `is_entry_point()` module and also strips `__DATA__`. As the golden diffs show, all non-entry-module output (allocator, builtins, internal structs) has disappeared. These goldens no longer capture optimizer output for prelude modules, so regressions there go unseen.

grade.reason: No finding addresses compile_one discarding the silent host's diagnostics or silently producing empty output when the dump returns None; finding 0 is about the shell script's --skip-empty hiding errors, which is a different root cause.

entries.defect: The .tagpr config put keys outside a [tagpr] section, where tagpr silently ignores them, and used `command` (which runs before the version bump) instead of `postVersionCommand`, so Cargo.lock was never synced and `cargo --locked` CI broke.

findings.summary: tagpr pushes the release tag with the default GITHUB_TOKEN, so the tag push never starts release.yml and no release gets published.
findings.detail: GitHub does not start new workflow runs for events caused by the repository GITHUB_TOKEN; it only allows workflow_dispatch and repository_dispatch. release.yml listens only for `push: tags: v*`, plus a manual workflow_dispatch. When the tagpr job merges the Release PR and pushes `vX.Y.Z` as github-actions, release.yml does not run, so the binaries and GitHub Release are never built. That breaks step 4 of the flow described in `.tagpr`. The fix is to use a PAT or GitHub App token, or to call the release jobs from tagpr.yml based on tagpr's `tag` output.

findings.summary: The Songmu/tagpr step does not set the GITHUB_TOKEN env var, which tagpr needs to call the GitHub API, so the job is likely to fail on every push to main.
findings.detail: The tagpr binary reads its credentials from the `GITHUB_TOKEN` environment variable. Its documented setup is `env: GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}` on the action step. The step here passes no env or token. tagpr then cannot open or update the Release PR or push tags, so every push to main gives a failing tagpr run and the release pipeline never starts.

findings.summary: tagpr's version-file regex is not line-anchored, so a version bump can also rewrite a dependency in [workspace.dependencies] that has the same version.
findings.detail: tagpr finds versions with a regex shaped like `(^|[^-_0-9a-zA-Z])version[^-_0-9a-zA-Z].{0,50}X.Y.Z`. Here `^` matches only the start of the file. It rewrites every match whose version equals the current one. So an inline table such as `lexopt = { version = "0.3.1" }` matches as well. When the workspace version reaches 0.3.1, the next Release PR would also change lexopt to 0.3.2, a version that may not exist. `cargo update --workspace` or the build would then fail. The comment's claim that the match is unambiguous is wrong.

grade.reason: No finding points out that the keys sit outside the [tagpr] section, or that `command` runs before the version bump so Cargo.lock is never synced; finding 2 concerns the regex anchoring, not this root cause.

findings.summary: tagpr pushes the release tag with the default GITHUB_TOKEN, so the tag push never starts release.yml and no release is ever published automatically.
findings.detail: GitHub does not start new workflow runs for events created with the repository GITHUB_TOKEN; it only makes an exception for workflow_dispatch and repository_dispatch. When the Release PR is merged, tagpr pushes `v<next>` using that token, so the `on: push: tags: ['v*']` trigger in release.yml does not fire. The flow described in .tagpr (step 4, 'release.yml runs on the tag push') therefore never happens, and every release would need someone to start workflow_dispatch by hand. The usual fixes are to give tagpr a PAT or GitHub App token, or to run the build/release jobs inside tagpr.yml, gated on tagpr's `tag` output.

findings.summary: The Songmu/tagpr step does not set a GITHUB_TOKEN environment variable, so tagpr may fail with no credentials.
findings.detail: tagpr reads its GitHub credentials from the GITHUB_TOKEN environment variable, and its documented usage passes `env: GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}` to the step. This workflow grants contents/pull-requests write permissions but never exposes the token to the action. If the action does not supply the token itself, every push to main will fail the tagpr job before it can open or update a Release PR.

findings.summary: The config assumes tagpr's version-file regex is line-anchored; if it is not, a version bump can also rewrite dependency versions in Cargo.toml.
findings.detail: The comment justifying `versionFile = Cargo.toml` claims tagpr only matches `version = "..."` at the start of a line. I have not checked tagpr's source. If its pattern only requires `version` to follow a non-identifier character, inline dependency entries such as `foo = { version = "x.y.z" }` in [workspace.dependencies] also match. Any dependency pinned to the same string as the current workspace version would then be silently rewritten on each bump. That would change a third-party dependency requirement, and the `cargo update --workspace` hook would pick it up.

grade.reason: No finding notes that the keys sit outside the [tagpr] section or that `command` runs before the version bump; the only .tagpr finding is about how the version regex matches.

findings.summary: The tagpr config is missing the `[tagpr]` section header, so none of its settings take effect and the file is probably invalid git-config.
findings.detail: tagpr reads `.tagpr` as a git-config file and looks up keys such as `tagpr.versionFile`, `tagpr.command` and `tagpr.release`. Here `versionFile`, `command` and `release` sit outside any section, which `git config` rejects as malformed. If tagpr fails on it, the tagpr job breaks on every push to main. If it doesn't, the keys are ignored: Cargo.toml is not used as the version file and `cargo update --workspace` never runs. Either way the release PR does not bump `[workspace.package].version` or sync Cargo.lock as intended.

findings.summary: `release = patch` gives the wrong kind of value to tagpr's `release` option, which controls whether a GitHub Release is created, not the bump size.
findings.detail: In tagpr, `tagpr.release` takes `true`, `draft` or `false` and decides whether tagpr itself publishes a GitHub Release. `patch` is not one of those values. Depending on how tagpr parses it, the run errors out or falls back to the default (`true`). With the default, tagpr publishes a release for the tag itself while release.yml is also building one, so the two compete over the same release.

findings.summary: release.yml never runs on its own for tags that tagpr creates, because tagpr pushes them with the default GITHUB_TOKEN.
findings.detail: tagpr.yml runs `Songmu/tagpr@v1` without a PAT or GitHub App token, so the tag push is authenticated with GITHUB_TOKEN. GitHub does not start new workflow runs for events created with GITHUB_TOKEN, so the `push: tags: v*` trigger in release.yml does not fire. Step 4 in the .tagpr comments never happens: no binaries are built or uploaded unless someone starts workflow_dispatch by hand.

findings.summary: tagpr's generic version-file replacement is not tied to the start of a line, so it can also rewrite dependency versions in Cargo.toml when they equal the workspace version.
findings.detail: The config comment says the regex only matches `version = "..."` at the start of a line. tagpr's generic replacer actually matches `version` followed within a few dozen characters by the current version string, anywhere on a line. Inline tables such as `foo = { version = "0.3" }` therefore count too. Once the workspace version equals a dependency's version string (for example both are 0.3.0, or a dependency is pinned to the same patch version), the release PR silently bumps that dependency requirement as well and can produce a broken or wrong manifest.

grade.reason: Finding 0 identifies that keys sit outside the [tagpr] section and are ignored, so `cargo update --workspace` never runs and Cargo.lock is not synced, which is the core root cause of the known defect, though it does not mention the command-vs-postVersionCommand timing.

entries.defect: The response body pump awaited `frame_tx.send` with no time bound, so a client that stopped draining but kept its connection open pinned the handler task's fiber stack forever.

findings.summary: Nothing caps the number of in-flight requests to the stack pool size, so heavy load runs out of fiber stacks: requests fail, and a recycle that hits the empty pool shuts the whole server down.
findings.detail: `create_serve_engine` sizes the pool with `total_stacks(max_concurrency)`. The only limit on work is `chan_cap = max_concurrency / workers`, and that limits the jobs waiting in each worker's channel, not the ones already running. `worker_loop` takes every job it receives and `accessor.spawn`s it into an unbounded `inflight` set, so the `workers` workers together can have far more than `max_concurrency` guest tasks holding stacks. The comment claiming 'never more in-flight work than the pooling allocator's stack pool was sized for' is wrong. Once the pool is empty, guest calls fail with 500s. A recycle's `instantiate_async`, which also needs a stack, fails too, and that path calls `fatal.notify_one()`, which shuts down the whole server.

findings.summary: The epoch deadline is only renewed when the dispatch loop turns, so a request that waits on host I/O longer than timeout+5s traps the shared store when it resumes and kills every in-flight request on that worker.
findings.detail: `set_epoch_deadline(epoch_ticks)` is renewed only after a new job arrives or an in-flight task finishes. Suppose a guest task is suspended on a host await, for example a slow outbound fetch or body back-pressure from a slow client, and the worker gets no other traffic for more than `timeout_secs+5` seconds. The epoch then passes the deadline while no wasm is running. When the guest resumes it traps immediately with `Trap::Interrupt`, `run_concurrent` returns `Err`, and every other request in flight on that long-lived store is lost. Before this change the epoch trap only affected that one request's own store.

findings.summary: The wall-clock bound on request execution is gone, so one stalled request can stop a worker during recycle or shutdown, and new requests then block forever in `submit` with no timeout.
findings.detail: The old `tokio::time::timeout` around `run_concurrent` was removed. A HandlerTask blocked on `frame_tx.send` (a client that stops reading) or on a host future that never resolves now stays in `inflight` indefinitely. Once the recycle threshold is reached, the worker stops taking jobs and waits for `inflight` to empty, which never happens. Its channel fills up. `Dispatch::submit` keeps routing every N-th request to that worker round-robin, and `dispatch_request` awaits `submit` before the first-byte timeout race starts, so those clients hang with no 504. Shutdown also waits up to `drain_deadline` for each such stuck task.

findings.summary: Switching serve to the pooling allocator without raising per-instance limits caps each instance's linear memory and GC heap at wasmtime's small pool default (10 MiB, recalled from wasmtime's source and not checked here), so apps that used to work now trap.
findings.detail: `PoolingAllocationConfig::new()` is used as-is; only the total counts are set. As I recall wasmtime's source (not verified against the 44.0.1 dependency), the pool's per-memory default `max_memory_size` is 10 MiB, and pooled GC heaps share that limit. Wado data lives in the Wasm GC heap, and instances now live for up to 10000 requests, so a guest whose linear memory or GC heap goes past that size gets a failed grow. The freelist allocator's `grow_memory` ignores the `memory_grow` result, so allocations past the limit write out of bounds, or GC allocation fails, and the request traps. With the old on-demand allocator memory had no such limit.

findings.summary: Any instantiation failure during a routine recycle or trap rebuild is treated as fatal and shuts the whole server down.
findings.detail: `worker_loop` calls `fatal.notify_one()` whenever `instantiate_async` fails, including the re-instantiation after a recycle or after a trap. This assumes failures are deterministic, but it also triggers on transient resource failures such as pool slot or stack exhaustion, or a guest global initializer that can fail at runtime. One failed rebuild ends the accept loop and takes down a server that was otherwise healthy.

grade.reason: Finding 2 points out that removing the wall-clock timeout leaves a HandlerTask blocked on `frame_tx.send` forever when the client stops reading, which pins the worker. This is the same root cause the fix addresses.

findings.summary: Requests are no longer bounded by a wall-clock timeout, and a worker that is recycling waits for in-flight requests with no limit. One stuck request can block the worker forever, and from then on every W-th request hangs in `Dispatch::submit`, which has no timeout of its own.
findings.detail: The old code wrapped `run_concurrent` in `tokio::time::timeout`, so a request blocked on a host await was dropped after `timeout`. Examples of such awaits are `frame_tx.send` against a client that keeps the socket open but stops reading, or a guest waiting for a request body that never arrives. That timeout was removed. The epoch deadline cannot help either: it only fires while wasm is running. When a worker hits `recycle_requests`, it sets `stopping` and waits only on `inflight.next()`, so a stuck request keeps it in the drain phase forever and it stops reading its channel. `Dispatch` keeps sending jobs round-robin to that worker. Once its bounded channel fills, `dispatch.submit(job).await` blocks forever, and the first-byte timeout only starts after `submit` returns. So any slow client that holds one request open across a recycle makes 1/W of all later requests hang with no 504.

findings.summary: `--max-concurrency` does not limit how many requests are in flight. Each worker moves jobs from its channel into `inflight` with no cap, so the fiber-stack pool sized from `max_concurrency` can run out under load.
findings.detail: `run_http_server` claims the per-worker queues (`chan_cap = max_concurrency / workers`) keep in-flight work within the pooling allocator's `total_stacks(max_concurrency)`. But `worker_loop` keeps calling `job_rx.recv()` and spawning a `HandlerTask` for each job, even while `inflight` is non-empty, with no upper bound. A channel's capacity limits queued jobs, not running ones. With more concurrent requests than `max_concurrency` (many slow or streaming responses, or a load test with more connections than the limit), more guest tasks need async fiber stacks than the pool holds. Stack allocation then fails and requests error out or the store fails. Instantiating a new instance during a recycle also needs a stack from the same pool.

findings.summary: A trap or runaway in one request now kills every concurrent request on the same worker, because all of them share one store and instance.
findings.detail: Before this change each request had its own `Store`, so a guest trap (a Wado `panic`, a failed `unwrap`, `unreachable`, or the epoch interrupt) only affected that request. Now all requests on a worker run as tasks inside one `run_concurrent`. When that store traps, `worker_loop` drops it together with every in-flight `HandlerTask`. Unrelated concurrent requests then get a 500 ('Handler aborted without producing a response') or a truncated streamed body, and the worker sleeps 100ms before rebuilding. The epoch deadline is also only pushed out when the dispatch loop turns. On a quiet worker whose single in-flight request sits in a host await for more than timeout+5s and then runs wasm again, the deadline has already passed. The resulting trap takes down all of that worker's requests, not just the slow one.

findings.summary: The double-free guard misses blocks that were coalesced into a neighbour, because their stale header still shows them as used; freeing such a block again corrupts the free lists.
findings.detail: When a freed block merges backward into a free predecessor, only the merged block's header and footer are rewritten (`fl_set_tags(prev, size, 0)`). The original block's header inside the merged region still holds `size|1`. Freeing that pointer again passes the `fl_used(header) == 0` check. The allocator then unlinks and coalesces using stale interior tags and pushes an overlapping block onto a bin. Two later allocations can then receive the same memory, which corrupts data silently instead of trapping.

grade.reason: Finding 0 names `frame_tx.send` blocking against a client that keeps the socket open but stops reading, and points out that the wall-clock timeout bounding it was removed, so the request stays stuck forever, which is the defect.

findings.summary: A Wado panic or other trap in one request is handled as a normal task error, so the worker keeps the same component instance; under wasmtime that instance is likely left unusable, and later requests on that worker could fail until it is recycled.
findings.detail: `HandlerTask::run` turns an `Err` from `service.handle` into `HandlerOutcome::Trapped` and returns `Ok(())`, so `run_concurrent` never fails and `worker_loop` does not rebuild the instance. A Wasm trap leaves the component instance in an unknown state. I expect wasmtime to reject further calls into it ('cannot enter component instance') — this rests on wasmtime's poisoning behaviour and was not checked against its source here. If so, every later request routed to that worker returns 500 until the recycle threshold (10000 requests by default; never when `--recycle-requests 0`). Before this change each request had its own store, so a trap (for example an `unwrap` on bad input) only affected that one request. Even if wasmtime surfaced the trap through `run_concurrent` instead, every other in-flight request on that worker would be dropped.

findings.summary: The epoch deadline is only pushed back when the dispatch loop turns, so a legitimately long request can trip it and the trap kills every in-flight request on that worker.
findings.detail: `set_epoch_deadline(epoch_ticks)` is called only when a new job arrives or an in-flight task finishes. Suppose a worker has one request waiting on host I/O or on body back-pressure (a slow client, a long download, streaming) for longer than timeout+5 s with no other traffic. The deadline passes, and the next time that guest runs wasm it gets an epoch trap. The trap makes `run_concurrent` return `Err`, which drops all other in-flight requests on the worker, not only the slow one. A healthy but long-lived request is treated as a runaway guest.

findings.summary: The per-request wall-clock timeout was removed, so a stuck request can stall a recycling worker forever, and requests sent to it hang with no timeout.
findings.detail: Before, `run_concurrent` was wrapped in `tokio::time::timeout`, which bounded each request even while it was blocked in a host await. Now a request stuck in `frame_tx.send` (the client stopped reading) or in a guest await that never completes stays in `inflight` indefinitely. When the worker reaches `recycle_requests` it stops reading `job_rx` and waits for `inflight` to drain, which never happens. Its channel then fills, and `dispatch.submit(job).await` in `dispatch_request` blocks forever, because the first-byte timeout only starts after submit returns. With round-robin dispatch, a fixed share of all incoming requests (1 in every `workers`) then hangs with no 504.

findings.summary: Switching `wado serve` to the pooling allocator with default per-instance limits caps each guest's linear memory and GC heap at the pool default, which wasmtime documents as roughly 10 MiB.
findings.detail: `PoolingAllocationConfig::new()` sets only instance, memory, table, heap and stack counts and leaves `max_memory_size` at its default (I believe 10 MiB; not checked against the pinned wasmtime version). Previously the on-demand allocator let memories grow up to the normal wasm limits. Services that use more than that fail `memory.grow`; `grow_memory` ignores the failure, so the next access is out of bounds and traps. GC-heavy Wado programs are hit hardest: instances now live for thousands of requests, so garbage builds up in a heap that may hit the cap and trap.

findings.summary: In-flight requests are not actually limited by `--max-concurrency`; only the queue length is, so the fiber-stack pool can run out.
findings.detail: `chan_cap = max_concurrency / workers` only limits how many jobs wait in each channel. The worker loop takes jobs off `job_rx` as fast as they arrive and spawns each into an unbounded `FuturesUnordered`, so a worker's in-flight count can grow far past `max_concurrency`. The stack pool was sized as `total_stacks(max_concurrency)`, on the assumption that in-flight work is bounded. Under load, stack allocation can fail and error the worker's `run_concurrent`, dropping every in-flight request on that worker.

entries.defect: The dataflow walker treated labeled blocks as straight-line code. It recorded no state at a labeled `break`, so the post-block state ignored early-exit paths that skipped syncs emitted inside the block. Later code then missed a re-read or write-back, and the field update was lost (the indent_level drift).

findings.summary: Labeled `break`s that leave the HFS loop no longer write the scalar back, and the post-loop write-back was removed, so the field's latest writes are lost.
findings.detail: `walk_stmt` calls `commit_scalar_for_escape` only for `return` and unlabeled `break`. `scalarize_loop` now returns an empty `post_stmts`, on the claim that every exit path has already committed. The inliner turns `return` into `break __inline_<fn>: v` (inline.rs:1545-1566). So when an inlined function's loop returns early, or a loop sits inside a user labeled block and does `break scope: v`, control leaves the loop in `ScalarOnly` state. No write-back runs on that path and no post-loop write-back exists, so every write since the last sync never reaches `obj.field`. Code after the loop then reads a stale field. Before this change the old post-loop write-back, plus the write-back before escaping breaks, covered this case.

findings.summary: Sync statements from inside an expression are all placed before the enclosing statement, so a re-read that should follow a `&mut` call runs before the call and the code reads a stale scalar.
findings.detail: `walk_expr` pushes re-reads, and the write-backs `walk_call_expr` adds before a call, into `out`, the list of statements emitted ahead of the current statement. Take a read that follows a call in the same expression, such as `if p.advance(&mut p) && p.pos < n`, `x = f(&mut s) + s.f`, or the right side of any binary or argument list. The call moves the state to `FieldOnly`, so the later read emits `__hfs_f = s.f`. That re-read goes before the whole statement and runs before the call. The read after the call then sees the value from before the call. The old code put the re-read after the statement, and the read itself never went to a stale scalar inside the expression. Only one call per statement got stmt-level sync, but this case was not miscompiled.

findings.summary: The state after a labeled block or inlined block comes from walking the block straight through, which ignores what holds when a `break <label>` jumps out early, so the code either reads a stale scalar or a re-read overwrites the value.
findings.detail: `TirStmtKind::LabeledBlock` and `TirExprKind::LabeledBlock` call `walk_block` and take the state at the end of the block's fall-through. A `break label` path can leave the block in a different state. Example: `lbl: { if c { s.f = 1; break lbl; } g(&mut s); }` followed by a read of `s.f`. The walker ends in `FieldOnly` and emits `__hfs_f = s.f`, which on the break path replaces the newly written 1 with the stale field. The reverse also happens. An inlined `&mut self` method that returns early (`break __inline_x`) while the state is `FieldOnly`, and then ends in `ScalarOnly` on fall-through, leads to a later read with no re-read on the break path, so the scalar is stale. The PR removed the `inline_block_written` guard that stopped such locals from being scalarized, so these inline-block shapes are now exposed.

findings.summary: `walk_nested_loop` computes the state after a nested loop from the inner body's end state, which may not match the state at the inner `break` that actually exits the loop.
findings.detail: A nested loop only exits through `break` or `return`. The state after it is set to JOIN(entry, body_exit_pre_sync). Consider an inner body like `g(&mut s); if done { break; } s.f = s.f + 1;`. At the break the state is `FieldOnly`: the scalar is stale, and `commit_scalar_for_escape` does nothing because it only handles `ScalarOnly`. The body end is `ScalarOnly`, so the join gives `ScalarOnly`. A later read of `s.f` in the outer loop gets no re-read and uses the stale scalar, losing g's update. When the outer body later writes back, g's change to the field is overwritten.

A later sibling read such as `b.v` in `let a = f(&mut b) + b.v;`, or `while p.advance() != 0 && p.pos < n`, then reaches the field-read branch of `walk_expr`, which pushes `make_re_read_stmt` into `out`. `out` holds statements placed before the enclosing statement, so the re-read runs before `f` and the read sees the old scalar. Take an inlined body like `__inline_X: { if c { g(&mut self); break __inline_X: v; } self.pos = e; ... }`. The `break` path reaches the block exit with `pos` in `FieldOnly`: the field is current and the scalar is stale. The walker instead assumes `ScalarOnly` after `self.pos = e`. Later `self.pos` reads in the loop get no re-read and use the stale scalar. The walker also adds convergence sync after the `break`, where it never runs. The code comment admits it does not track break-target states.

Suppose the match is entered `ScalarOnly` (a field write earlier in the loop body) and a guard calls `probe(&mut b)`. The guard's prefix writes back and the call leaves `FieldOnly`, yet later arms are analysed as `ScalarOnly`. Their reads of `b.v` use `__hfs_v` without a re-read and miss `probe`'s change. The new fixture only passes because the match is entered in `Both`.

entries.defect: can_move_past only checked whether the intervening statement clobbers the moved expression's reads, not the reverse; a call-containing field initializer could therefore be relocated past an intervening read of a global it mutates, a miscompile.

findings.summary: `can_move_past` only checks whether the intervening statement's writes clobber the inner expression's reads. It never checks whether the inner expression's own writes, calls or allocations conflict with what the intervening statement reads or writes, so side-effecting initializers can be moved past statements they depend on.
findings.detail: The new pass explicitly does not require the inner field initializer to be pure. It may contain a `Call`, `LocalSet`/`LocalTee`, `GlobalSet`, `StructSet` or a memory store. `can_move_past` only calls `int_mr.may_clobber(expr_mr)`. Example: `self = struct.new Box{ value: g() }; y = obj.f; use(self.value)`. If `g` changes `obj.f`, the rewrite makes `y` read the old value. A second example: `self = struct.new Box{ value: local.tee x (...) }; y = x; use(self.value)`. Here `y` now sees the old `x`. The reverse check `expr_mr.may_clobber(int_mr)` is missing, and so are write-after-write conflicts on locals, globals, heap and memory.

findings.summary: Two calls can be reordered. When the inner initializer is a call with no arguments, `may_clobber` treats it as read-free, so an intervening statement that also calls is allowed through and the order of the two calls' side effects is swapped.
findings.detail: `may_clobber` returns true for `self.calls` only when `!other.is_read_free()`. A summary like `Call { args: [] }` (for example `self = struct.new Box{ value: next_id() }`) has no reads recorded, even though the callee can read and write anything. If the next sibling is `print(...)` or any other call, `can_move_past` accepts it and the inner call is moved after it. This changes observable output order and state. Calls inside the expression should be treated as both reading and writing everything.

findings.summary: The trap-ordering check ignores calls. `may_trap` is never set for `Call`/`CallRef`/`CallIndirect`, so an inner call can be reordered with a trapping intervening statement, or a trapping inner with an intervening call.
findings.detail: Callees can trap (unreachable, out-of-bounds access, etc.) and can have observable effects before trapping. With `inner = f()`, which prints and then traps, and an intervening `y = a / b` that traps on zero, `can_move_past` sees `expr_mr.may_trap == false` and allows the move. The program then traps on the division before `f` prints, which changes observable output. The reverse case is also wrong: a trapping inner (for example a `StructGet` on null) moved past an intervening call that has observable effects lets the call's effects happen before the trap.

findings.summary: The inner expression's control effect is never checked. An initializer containing `Br`/`Return`/`Unreachable`, or a conditional block, is moved past intervening statements that originally never ran when the inner exited.
findings.detail: `can_move_past` requires `int_mr.control == Linear` but places no condition on `expr_mr.control`. If the field initializer is a `Block` that can `return` or branch out (for example an inlined early-exit or a panic path ending in `Unreachable`), the original program skipped the intervening statements on that path. After the rewrite those statements run first, which can perform writes that were never meant to happen. Previously this was harmless because only `Nop`s were skipped.

findings.detail: The pass no longer requires the inner initializer to be pure, so it may contain a `Call`, a `LocalTee`/`LocalSet` inside a block, a `GlobalSet`, a `StructSet`/`ArraySet` or a memory store. `can_move_past` only evaluates `int_mr.may_clobber(expr_mr)`. Example: inner = `{ g = g + 1; g }` (or a call that updates a global) and intervening = `y = global.get g`. Before the rewrite `y` sees the updated value; after the inner moves to the use site, `y` sees the old value. Local writes inside the inner are just as unsafe: an intervening `y = x` read before the inner's `x` write, or a write to the same local, gets reordered. Write-after-read and write-after-write dependencies are lost, which gives wrong results.

findings.summary: Two calls can swap order when the moved initializer is a call with no reads, for example `f()` with no arguments, and the intervening statement is another call such as `println`.
findings.detail: In `may_clobber`, an intervening call only counts as a clobber when `!other.is_read_free()`. An inner like `Call { args: [] }` reads nothing, `Call` does not set `may_trap`, and the intervening call is `Control::Linear`. `can_move_past` therefore returns true and the inner call is moved after the intervening call. Two calls with observable effects (I/O, global mutation, panics) now run in the opposite order. The same gap lets a heap/memory-writing inner with no reads move past an intervening heap/memory write, so a write-after-write is reordered.

findings.summary: The trap-ordering rule only rejects the move when both sides may trap. A side-effecting inner can therefore be moved past an intervening statement that traps, or past a call that never returns, and its effects are lost.
findings.detail: If the inner performs a call, an allocation or a write without trapping itself, and the intervening statement may trap (for example `y = a / b`, or an array or struct access) or is a call that may panic or loop forever, the original program ran the inner's side effects before the trap. After the rewrite the trap or panic happens first and the effects (output, global or heap updates) never occur. The doc comment claims the 'surviving trap fires at its own point', but that only holds when the moved expression has no effects.

entries.defect: inflate_get_gzip_header converted each FNAME/FCOMMENT byte to its own char (Latin-1 style), while gzip_compress_with_header wrote the names' UTF-8 bytes, so non-ASCII names and comments came back as mojibake.

findings.summary: Preset-dictionary compression emits the dictionary itself as part of the compressed stream, so standard zlib decoders return the dictionary bytes in front of the data.
findings.detail: `DeflateStream::compress_zlib` and `compress_raw` join `dict + input`, deflate the whole buffer and (for zlib) compute the Adler-32 trailer over the joined bytes. In real zlib a preset dictionary only primes the LZ77 window: the dictionary is never encoded and the checksum covers only the data. Any standard inflater, including zlib-rs given the dictionary, returns `dict ++ data`, not the original data. The Wado side has the matching problem: `InflateStream::decompress_zlib` does not preload the window with the dictionary, then drops the first `dict.len()` output bytes. Real FDICT streams that use back-references into the dictionary therefore fail with an invalid distance and an adler32 mismatch, or decode wrong. The DICTID field is also never checked against the dictionary.

findings.summary: Lazy matching re-inserts the current position into the hash chain, creating a self-loop that drops older candidates and burns up to `max_chain` iterations per lookup.
findings.detail: In `deflate_with_level`, `pos` is inserted into the chain (`prev[pos]=head[h]; head[h]=pos`) before the deferred match is decided. When the previous match is then emitted, the insert loop starts at `i = 0` and inserts `pos` again. That sets `prev[pos % 32768] = head[h] == pos`, a cycle on itself. Any later chain walk that reaches this position keeps re-visiting it, repeating the byte comparison until `chain_count` reaches `max_chain` (4096 at level 9). All older match candidates behind it are lost. The same loop also fails to insert the last position of the match (`pos + skip - 1`). The result is much slower compression and worse ratios at levels 4 to 9.

findings.summary: `inflate_get_gzip_header` decodes FNAME and FCOMMENT bytes as Unicode code points, which garbles any non-ASCII name or comment.
findings.detail: `bytes_to_string` appends `buf[i] as char` for each byte. A byte of 0x80 or above becomes U+0080..U+00FF and is re-encoded as two UTF-8 bytes. A header written by `gzip_compress_with_header` from a UTF-8 name, which emits the raw bytes via `get_byte`, therefore reads back differently. For example "café" comes back as "cafÃ©".

findings.summary: `Z_DEFAULT_COMPRESSION` is defined as 6 instead of zlib's -1, and out-of-range levels such as -1 are silently treated as level 9.
findings.detail: In zlib, `Z_DEFAULT_COMPRESSION` is -1 and means level 6. Here the constant is 6, and `get_deflate_config` maps any level outside 0 to 8, including -1, to the level-9 settings (`max_chain` 4096). Code ported from zlib that passes -1 gets very slow level-9 compression. `zlib_wrap` and the gzip XFL field then report a level hint that does not match the work done, and no error is raised for invalid levels.

findings.summary: Level 0 compression of empty input produces a deflate stream with no blocks, which standard decoders reject.
findings.detail: `deflate_with_level` returns `deflate_stored(input)` for level 0 before it reaches the empty-input check. `deflate_stored`'s loop `while pos < total` never runs when `total == 0`, so it emits no block at all, not even a final empty stored block. As a result, `compress2(&[], 0)`, `gzip_compress2(&[], 0)`, `deflate_raw2(&[], 0)` and a `DeflateStream` at level 0 all produce a zlib, gzip or raw stream with no BFINAL block. Wado's own inflate tolerates this because it stops when input runs out, but zlib, zlib-rs and flate2 fail with an incomplete or truncated stream error.

findings.summary: Preset-dictionary zlib streams are not zlib-compatible: the dictionary bytes are compressed into the stream and covered by the Adler-32, and inflate cannot use a real dictionary.
findings.detail: `DeflateStream::compress_zlib` concatenates dict+input, deflates the whole buffer, sets FDICT, and writes the Adler-32 of the combined buffer. In real zlib the dictionary only seeds the window: it is never emitted, and the trailer checksums only the data. So a standard inflater given the dictionary outputs dict+data. In the other direction, `InflateStream::decompress_zlib` never loads `self.dict` into the inflate window; it just skips the dictionary ID and later strips `dict_len` bytes from the output. Real FDICT streams from zlib/zlib-rs use back-references into the dictionary, which hit the `win_copy > whave` → INF_BAD path, so they decode to truncated or wrong data and then fail the Adler-32 check. Separately, the dictionary ID is never compared with the dictionary the caller supplied.

findings.summary: In RAW_FORMAT, setting a preset dictionary makes decompression return the dictionary bytes in front of the data.
findings.detail: `DeflateStream::compress_raw` deflates dict+input when `has_dict` is set, so the stream literally contains the dictionary. Nothing on the inflate side removes it: `InflateStream::decompress` for RAW_FORMAT calls `inflate_raw(input)`, and so does any external raw inflater. A RAW_FORMAT round-trip with a dictionary therefore returns dict+data instead of data.

findings.summary: Lazy matching re-inserts the current position into its own hash chain, creating a self-loop that cuts the chain and wastes up to max_chain iterations.
findings.detail: In the lazy branch of `deflate_with_level` (levels 4-9), the current `pos` has already been inserted earlier in the same iteration (`prev[pos%32768] = head[h]; head[h] = pos`). When the previous match is emitted, the loop `for i = 0; i < skip - 1` inserts position `pos + 0` again. That sets `prev[pos] = head[h] = pos`, a self-reference. Every later search reaching this node keeps revisiting the same candidate, repeating a match comparison of up to 258 bytes, until `chain_count` hits `max_chain` (4096 at level 9). Older chain entries become unreachable. The result is worse compression and a large slowdown on repetitive data. The non-lazy paths correctly start this loop at `i = 1`.

findings.summary: `inflate_get_gzip_header` turns non-ASCII FNAME/FCOMMENT bytes into different strings.
findings.detail: `bytes_to_string` appends `` `{buf[offset + i] as char}` `` for each byte. A byte of 0x80 or above becomes a Latin-1 code point and is encoded as two UTF-8 bytes. A UTF-8 file name such as "ä.txt" therefore comes back as mojibake with a different length, so the original header fields cannot be recovered or round-tripped through `gzip_compress_with_header`.

findings.summary: Preset-dictionary compression writes the dictionary bytes into the compressed stream itself instead of using them only as the starting history window.
findings.detail: `DeflateStream::compress_zlib` (and `compress_raw`) joins `dict + input`, deflates the whole buffer and computes the Adler-32 trailer over `combined`. Real zlib with FDICT uses the dictionary only as the initial window: the dictionary is not part of the output, and the trailer covers the input data alone. A standard inflater (zlib, zlib-rs, flate2) given this stream and the dictionary decodes without error but returns `dict` followed by the data, because the dictionary bytes are encoded as literals and the checksum matches the joined buffer. The data is silently wrong. The FDICT test only checks the header bit and does not cross-decompress.

findings.summary: `InflateStream::decompress_zlib` never loads the preset dictionary into the inflate window, does not check DICTID, and drops the first `dict.len()` bytes of real output.
findings.detail: When FDICT is set, the code skips the 4-byte DICTID without comparing it to `adler32(dict)` and calls `inflate_raw_from` with an empty window. A standard zlib FDICT stream refers back into the dictionary with match distances, so these back-references fail (`win_copy > whave` gives INF_BAD). Output is cut short and the call ends in an adler32 mismatch panic. If the stream happens not to reference the dictionary, the code still drops `dict_len` bytes of real data. A wrong dictionary is never reported. It only round-trips with Wado's own non-standard encoder.

findings.summary: RAW_FORMAT with a preset dictionary does not round-trip: the decompressed output begins with the dictionary bytes.
findings.detail: `DeflateStream::compress_raw` deflates `dict + input` when `has_dict` is set. `InflateStream::decompress` for RAW_FORMAT calls `inflate_raw(input)`, which neither uses nor removes the dictionary. Compressing data X with dictionary D and decompressing it with the same dictionary returns D followed by X instead of X.

findings.summary: The lazy matcher reinserts the current position into the hash chain, so `prev[pos]` points at `pos` and the chain loops on itself.
findings.detail: When the deferred match is emitted, `pos` has already been inserted (`prev[pos]=head[h]; head[h]=pos`). The skip loop then starts at `i = 0` and inserts `pos` again, setting `prev[pos % 32768] = head[mh]`, which is `pos`. Any later chain walk that reaches this node gets the same `chain` back with a positive `dist`. It spins on that node until `max_chain` is used up and never reaches older candidates. Levels 4-9 compress worse and waste search time (up to 4096 useless iterations at level 9). The last position of the match, `pos+skip-1`, is also never inserted.

findings.summary: `uncompress2` checks `max_output` only after decompressing the whole input, so it does not protect against decompression bombs.
findings.detail: `uncompress2` calls `uncompress(input)`, which inflates everything into memory, and only then compares `result.len() > max_output`. A small malicious input can expand to gigabytes and exhaust memory before the limit is ever checked, which defeats the purpose of an output size limit.

findings.summary: `inflate_get_gzip_header` corrupts non-ASCII file names and comments.
findings.detail: `bytes_to_string` turns each byte into a `char` and formats it, so a byte ≥ 0x80 becomes a separate Unicode scalar (Latin-1) and is re-encoded as two UTF-8 bytes. A UTF-8 name written by `gzip_compress_with_header` (which writes the raw bytes from `get_byte`) is therefore not returned unchanged; the name and comment fields come back corrupted.

entries.defect: write_atomic named its temp file only by process id, so concurrent threads in one process writing the same cache path shared one temp file and could rename it out from under each other, causing failed writes.

findings.summary: The options descriptor read back from a registry generator's WIT keeps the WIT kebab-case field and enum-case names, so options written with normal Wado snake_case or PascalCase names fail validation.
findings.detail: `record_descriptor` copies `field.name` and `options_type` copies `c.name` straight from the component WIT, where they are kebab-case (`max-depth`, `high-contrast`). `options_check::validate` matches the use-site keys exactly against these names (`provided.get(&field.name)` and the unknown-field check). The enum check is an exact `variants.iter().any(|v| v == s)`. So `options: { max_depth: 3, mode: "HighContrast" }` gives an 'unknown options field `max_depth`' error plus a 'required field `max-depth` missing' error. The case name is also rejected. The runtime side expects the opposite: `kiln_runtime::canonical_to_val` converts raw Wado names with `to_kebab` before matching the record fields and enum cases. As a result, any registry generator whose options have a multi-word field or a multi-word/PascalCase enum case cannot be configured the same way as its source-compiled form.

findings.summary: `write_atomic` names its temp file only by process id, so two concurrent writers in the same process share and clobber one temp file.
findings.detail: The temp path is `path.with_extension(format!("tmp-{}", std::process::id()))`. Compiles inside one process can run concurrently: `wado test` compiles fixtures in parallel and shares the Kiln cache. If two of them pull the same cold component or generator, both truncate and write the same temp file. The first `rename` publishes a file the second writer is still truncating or writing, so another reader can see a half-written `component.wasm` — exactly what the comment says cannot happen. The second `rename` then fails with ENOENT. In `dep_component::pull_component` that error propagates and fails the compile with 'writing …: No such file or directory'. The temp name needs a per-call unique part, such as a counter or a random suffix.

findings.summary: A registry generator is pulled by its mutable tag and run at build time without checking the lock's integrity digest.
findings.detail: `wado update` records `integrity` (the manifest digest) for each `[[build-dependency]]`, but `locked_generator_versions` only reads the version. `resolve_spec` and `fetch_build_dependencies` pull `world_reference(..., &version)` by tag and write the bytes to the shared cache. Nothing compares them with the locked digest. If the tag is re-pushed or the registry is compromised, different generator code is executed during compilation, while the lock claims a pinned artifact. That code is then cached permanently under `~/wado/` and trusted on every later build.

findings.summary: A locked generator version is used even when it no longer satisfies the manifest's version requirement, and the lock lookup ignores which registry the entry came from.
findings.detail: `resolve_build_dependencies` and `CliGeneratorProvider::resolve_version` return `locked.get(package)` without checking it against the `[build-dependencies]` requirement. Nothing compares `deps_hash` for staleness either. If a user changes `"wado-lang:gale" = { version = "^0.1" }` but leaves the old lock pinning 0.0.9, compile and fetch silently use 0.0.9. `locked_generator_versions` also keys only by the `ns:pkg` tail of the id, dropping the registry URL. So a lock entry from one registry pins a same-named package declared against another registry. The LSP code was deliberately written to avoid that by matching the full lock id.

findings.summary: The options descriptor read from a registry generator keeps the WIT kebab-case field and enum case names. Use-site validation compares against Wado names, so any multi-word option field or enum case is rejected.
findings.detail: `record_descriptor` stores `field.name` and `options_type` stores `e.cases[..].name` exactly as WIT has them (`max-depth`, `high-contrast`).
