findings.summary: Importing a component that exports a world-level function whose signature is not just primitives or strings (list, option, result, tuple, record) now crashes the compiler instead of reporting an error, even when the consumer never calls that function.
findings.detail: `build_bindings` used to reject world-level function exports with a clear error. It now accepts every one and emits a binding for it. `resolve_import_plan` Phase 4 adds every registered world function to the plan without checking whether it is used. `generate_cm_world_func_imports` then passes each signature to `wado_type_to_cm_val_type` with empty type maps, and that function panics on `List`/`Option`/tuple and on any named type (`unsupported generic param type for CM`). The doc comment says such signatures are "rejected", but no code rejects them. So `use { Iface } from "./dep.wasm"` on a dependency that also exports `fn f(x: list<u8>)` crashes with an internal compiler error where it used to give a diagnostic.

findings.summary: Calls to world-level functions from a dependency that imports WASI capabilities are treated as pure, so missing-effect errors are never reported and the dependency's imports are left out of the import list.
findings.detail: `register_component_decls` records host-leaf imports only for `interface_fqs`, never for `world_func_names`. The world-function adapter also has its effects cleared (`produced.adapter.borrow_mut().effects.clear()`). On top of that, `imported_cm_interface_fqs` skips `ImportKind::WorldFunction` on the assumption that the dependency is pure. A component that exports only world functions but imports e.g. `wasi:cli/stdout` (or a guest interface) therefore needs no effect from its caller, gets no missing-effect diagnostic, and its surviving imports are missing from the list the WIT producer reads. The composed binary and the WIT world embedded in it then disagree.

findings.summary: World-level function imports are keyed only by their snake_case name, so two dependencies that export a function with the same name overwrite each other.
findings.detail: `register_world_import` stores into `effect_to_func`/`world_import_functions`, and `register_component_decls` stores into `world_import_sources`, all keyed by the bare Wado name. When a second dependency exports the same name (e.g. `highlight`), its entry replaces the first one's. Calls to the first dependency's function fail the `world_import_source == module_source` check and are not rewritten to the adapter, so they become an unresolved bodyless call. Composition also lists the CM name for both assets and imports it from both, so the wiring or encoding is wrong.

findings.summary: The guest-effect name collision check rejects any `--lib` build whose entry declares an effect named like the package, even when the effect is handled inside the library and never becomes an import.
findings.detail: `register_lib_guest_effect_imports` runs for every `--lib` build. It collects every entry-module `interface` that has no `#[cm]` methods and errors if its kebab name equals the library's interface name. It does not check whether the effect actually escapes the library boundary. A package `json` with an internal `interface Json` that is fully handled (`with h do { ... }`) used to compile and now fails with "collides with the library's own interface name".

findings.summary: The LSP always passes an empty provided-import set to `check_semantics`, so files that use `with { provider: ... }` show false missing-effect errors in the editor.
findings.detail: The batch compiler builds a provider for each `provider:` directive and passes its FQs to `check_semantics`, which discharges the reconstructed guest effect. The LSP never resolves providers and passes `IndexSet::default()`. Code such as `provider_surface.wado` (calling `Hlc::wrap` with no handler) compiles fine but shows "missing effect 'Highlight'" in the editor.

findings.summary: A guest interface satisfied by a composed provider is still listed as a surviving import, and the provider's own imports are left out.
findings.detail: For `ImportKind::Component` entries, `imported_cm_interface_fqs` copies every host-leaf import of the dependency, including the guest FQ (e.g. `test:hlc/highlight@0.1.0`). The provided set (`options.providers`) is never consulted, and the provider's own imports (e.g. WASI) are never added. The WIT producer reads this flat list, so the world it describes or embeds does not match the composed binary, which no longer imports the guest interface but may import whatever the provider needs.

grade.reason: No finding describes compose_dependency_components failing with 'no composed dependency imports provider interface' when a provider's dependency was dead-code-eliminated; the provider-related findings cover import lists and LSP effects instead.

findings.summary: If a provider is supplied but its dependency is not composed, `compose_dependency_components` bails and the compiler panics.
findings.detail: The early return now happens only when `providers` is also empty. A dependency is instantiated only if the program still imports at least one of its exported interfaces or functions after DCE. Suppose the calls into the dependency are only inside `test` blocks, as in `provider_surface.wado` built without test mode, or only in unused functions. Then `dep_instances` stays empty, the provider loop hits `bail!("no composed dependency imports provider interface ...")`, and the `Err` arm turns that into `panic!("failed to compose CM component dependencies")`. The user gets an ICE instead of a component.

findings.summary: World-level function imports only support primitives and strings; any other type in an imported component's world function crashes codegen with a panic.
findings.detail: `build_bindings` no longer rejects world-level function exports. `generate_cm_world_func_imports` calls `wado_type_to_cm_val_type` with empty enum/flags/borrow maps and no stream or result type indices. A world function that takes or returns `list<..>`, `option<..>`, `result<..>`, a record, enum or variant hits `panic!("unsupported Wado param type for CM")` or `expect("result param type not defined")`. The doc comment says such signatures are rejected, but nothing produces that diagnostic. `resolve_import_plan` Phase 4 also pushes every registered world function whether or not it is called, so importing such a component crashes the build even if the function is never used.

findings.summary: World-function adapters are always made effect-free, so the dependency's WASI or guest-effect imports never reach the consumer's effect check.
findings.detail: `generate_import_adapters` clears every effect on a world-function adapter. `register_component_decls` records host-leaf imports only under the interface FQs, so a dependency that exports only world functions has no reconstructed effects. If that dependency imports `wasi:cli`, the filesystem, or a guest interface like `test:hlc/highlight`, a consumer calls the function with no matching effect or handler and gets no 'missing effect' diagnostic. Those imports also survive composition and are not listed in `imported_cm_interface_fqs` (the `WorldFunction` arm adds nothing), so the emitted WIT and the binary disagree.

findings.summary: An interface satisfied by a provider is still reported as an import of the composed artifact.
findings.detail: For `ImportKind::Component`, `imported_cm_interface_fqs` adds every host-leaf import of the dependency, now including the non-WASI guest interface. When a provider satisfies that interface, `wasm-compose` removes the import from the binary, but `imported_cm_interfaces` (used by the WIT producer and the import-plan faithfulness check) still lists it. The embedded or emitted WIT then declares an import the component does not have.

findings.summary: Two `provider` directives on the same dependency create duplicate providers, and the second wiring makes composition fail with a panic.
findings.detail: `resolve_inline_providers` makes one job per `use` decl across all loaded modules and does not deduplicate by dependency or FQ. If two modules import the same `.wasm` with a `provider`, two `ProviderComponent`s with the same `import_fq` are added. Each one is connected to the same dependency import, so the second `graph.connect` fails and `compose_dependency_components` panics. The provider is also compiled twice.

findings.summary: World-function imports are keyed only by bare name, so two dependencies exporting a function with the same name overwrite each other.
findings.detail: `register_world_import` and `world_import_sources` are maps keyed by the snake-case function name. If two composed components both export a world-level `highlight`, the second registration replaces the first. Calls to the first dependency's function then fail the `world_import_source(name) == Some(module_source)` check and are never retargeted to an adapter, which leaves an unresolved call or ICE. The single registered CM import is also composed from whichever asset happens to match.

findings.summary: The `--implement` option exists in the documentation and option structs, but the CLI cannot actually set it.
findings.detail: `parse_args` always sets `lib_interface_export: false`, and no `--implement` flag is parsed anywhere. A provider component cannot be built from the CLI as documented. Exports stay ungrouped unless a signature names a type, so the built artifact does not export the interface FQ that composition looks up with `export_by_name(fq)`.

grade.reason: Finding 0 describes the same defect: when the dependency is eliminated by DCE, `dep_instances` stays empty and the provider loop bails with 'no composed dependency imports provider interface', which causes a panic.

findings.summary: A `provider:` on a dependency that ends up not composed crashes the compiler instead of reporting an error.
findings.detail: `compose_dependency_components` adds a dependency to `dep_instances` only when the import plan uses one of its exports or world functions. Providers are wired unconditionally. Suppose a user writes `use { Hlc } from "./hlc.wasm" with { provider: "./p.wado" }` and never calls `Hlc`, or the call is removed as dead code. Then no composed dependency imports the provider interface, the code hits `bail!("no composed dependency imports provider interface ...")`, and the `match compose()` turns that into `panic!("failed to compose CM component dependencies")`, an internal compiler error. The same panic happens when two `use` decls (for example in different modules) give a provider for the same dependency: both providers try to connect to the same dependency import and `graph.connect` fails.

findings.summary: World-level function exports with list/option/result/tuple/record types are now accepted at binding time and then crash codegen.
findings.detail: Before this change, `build_bindings` returned a clean error for any `WorldItem::Function`. Now `emit_world_function` accepts every signature and maps it with `map_type`. `generate_cm_world_func_imports` then converts the types with `wado_type_to_cm_val_type` using empty type-index maps and no stream/result indices. Any world function whose signature uses `list<..>`, `option<..>`, `tuple`, `result` or a named record/variant/enum hits `panic!("unsupported ... type for CM")` or `expect("result param type not defined")`. The doc comment says such signatures are rejected, but nothing rejects them, so a user diagnostic became an ICE.

findings.summary: The LSP reports a false 'missing effect' error for every call into a dependency whose guest effect is satisfied by `with { provider: ... }`.
findings.detail: The batch compiler collects `provided_import_fqs` from `options.providers`, which includes inline `provider:` directives, and passes them to `check_semantics`, so the reconstructed guest effect is discharged. The LSP always passes an empty `IndexSet` and never resolves inline providers. Code that compiles, such as `provider_surface.wado` calling `Hlc::wrap` with no handler, therefore shows a 'missing effect Highlight' error in the editor.

findings.summary: A dependency's non-WASI import now becomes an effect that a local `with h do` handler satisfies at check time, but the handler never runs.
findings.detail: `build_bindings` now turns each non-WASI import interface into a `#[cm]` interface, so effect reconstruction requires that effect and a user handler discharges it. Codegen still passes the dependency's import up to the consumer's own imports (`imported_cm_interface_fqs` copies `host_leaf_imports_for`), and nothing wires the handler to the dependency. The effect check accepts the program, but at runtime the dependency calls whatever the host supplies for that import (or fails to instantiate), and the user's handler is silently ignored. Separately, components that relied on the host satisfying a custom non-WASI import now fail with 'missing effect' unless a handler or provider is given.

findings.summary: A component that both imports and exports the same non-WASI interface loses that export and gets duplicate synthesized declarations.
findings.detail: `component_interface_fqs` now drops every exported FQ that also appears in the host-leaf import list. For a wrapper/middleware component that exports `x:y/z` and also imports `x:y/z`, the export is never registered as a component interface or composed, so consumer calls to it are not wired. `build_bindings` also emits the same interface twice (once for the export loop, once for the new import loop), which gives duplicate items in the binding module.

findings.summary: World-function imports are keyed globally by bare snake-case name, so two dependencies exporting the same name overwrite each other.
findings.detail: `register_world_import` inserts into `effect_to_func` and `world_import_functions` under the bare name, and `register_component_decls` overwrites `world_import_sources[name]`. If two imported components both export a world-level `highlight`, the last registration wins. Calls into the other dependency no longer match `world_import_source(&func.name) == Some(&func.module_source)` and are not rewritten to an adapter. In composition, both assets also match the same CM name and both try to connect to the single program import, which makes `graph.connect` fail and panic.

grade.reason: Finding 0 describes how a dependency that was never called or was dead-code-eliminated is left out of dep_instances, which triggers the 'no composed dependency imports provider interface' bail and makes compilation fail.

entries.defect: walk_and_delete propagated NotFound errors from read_dir, the directory entries, file_type and remove_file, so a file or directory removed concurrently during output reconcile aborted the whole pipeline with an I/O error.

findings.summary: `cache_matches` never checks the generator identity or the output directory, so after a generator version bump or an `output-dir` change the stale cached outputs are reused.
findings.detail: The cache entry is looked up by invocation name, and the only extra check is `options_hash`. `cache_matches` compares the primary file, the inputs, the reads and the recorded output paths, but never compares `entry.generator` with `generator_identity(&invocation.module)`. It also never checks that the recorded outputs sit under the invocation's current `output_dir`. Two cases go wrong. (1) Changing `module = "ns:proto@1.0.0"` to `@2.0.0` with unchanged schemas is a cache hit, so code from the old generator is kept. (2) Changing `output-dir` is also a cache hit, because the old files still exist at their recorded paths. The new directory is never populated, and `kept_by_dir` records the old paths under the new directory key, so the old directory is never reconciled either.

findings.summary: The generator's `host::read-file` goes straight to `FilesystemCompilerHost::load_source`, which runs `base_path.join(path)` with no confinement, so a generator can read any file on the host.
findings.detail: `KilnHostState::read_file` passes the path supplied by the guest to `self.host.load_source(&path)`. In wado-lsp, `load_source` does `self.base_path.join(path)`. For an absolute path such as `/home/u/.ssh/id_rsa`, `join` replaces the base entirely, and `../..` segments walk out of the project. A generator pulled in as a build dependency can therefore read secrets and embed them in the generated sources. This breaks the sandbox the module claims to provide (only two host imports, deterministic execution). Input paths are never checked to be relative and free of `..`.

findings.summary: Nested output directories are reconciled separately, so reconciling the outer directory deletes the inner invocation's freshly generated files.
findings.detail: `run_pipeline` groups kept paths by the exact `output_dir` string and calls `reconcile_outputs` once per directory. `walk_and_delete` recurses into every subdirectory. Take invocation A with `output-dir = "gen"` and invocation B with `output-dir = "gen/sub"`. Reconciling `gen` walks into `gen/sub`, finds B's files with the `#![generated]` marker, sees they are not in A's kept list, and deletes them. The lockfile still records B's outputs, so the next run gets a cache miss, or a build that just ran has its outputs missing.

findings.summary: Read paths are run through `InvocationPath::normalize` before they are stored and checked, which drops a leading `/` and changes which file the cache check loads.
findings.detail: `build_cache_entry` stores `InvocationPath::normalize(&r.path)`, and `cache_matches` loads the normalized path again. `normalize` filters out empty segments, so a generator read of `/abs/x.proto` is recorded as `abs/x.proto`. On the next run that resolves to `<root>/abs/x.proto`, a different file. If that file does not exist, the cache misses on every run. If it does exist, freshness is judged against an unrelated file, so a change to the real file can go undetected.

findings.summary: A missing file is reported to the generator as `io(...)` rather than `not-found`, because the CLI host never returns `SourceError::NotFound`.
findings.detail: `read_file` maps only `SourceError::NotFound` to `HostError::NotFound`. The CLI host goes through `wado_lsp::FilesystemCompilerHost::load_source`, which turns every `std::fs::read` error, ENOENT included, into `SourceError::IoError`. A generator that handles optional includes by checking for `not-found` gets a generic I/O error instead and may fail the build.

findings.summary: If the guest traps or runs out of fuel, the diagnostics it emitted are thrown away.
findings.detail: `call_generate(...).await.map_err(...)?` returns early on a trap, so the loop that drains `diagnostics` and relays them to the host never runs. Messages emitted before a crash or fuel exhaustion, often the ones that explain the failure, are silently lost.

grade.reason: No finding addresses walk_and_delete propagating NotFound errors when files or directories are removed concurrently; finding 2 concerns nested output directories being deleted, not concurrent-removal error tolerance.

findings.summary: A generator's `read-file` import goes straight to `FilesystemCompilerHost::load_source`, which uses `base_path.join(path)`, so a generator can read any file on the machine.
findings.detail: `read_file` passes the path it gets from the guest to `self.host.load_source(&path)` without checking it. `wado_lsp::FilesystemCompilerHost::load_source` builds the path with `self.base_path.join(path)`. An absolute path replaces the base, and `..` segments are kept. A third-party generator from `[build-dependencies]` can therefore read `/etc/passwd`, `~/.ssh/id_rsa` or anything else the user can read, and put the bytes into its generated output. The module docs promise that only these two host imports are linked so generators stay sandboxed; this breaks that promise.

findings.summary: `cache_matches` never compares the recorded generator identity, so changing `module = "ns:x@1.0.0"` to a new version reuses stale outputs.
findings.detail: `run_pipeline` reuses the prior entry when `options_hash` matches and `cache_matches` returns true. `cache_matches` only checks the primary, inputs, reads and output hashes. It never compares `entry.generator` with `generator_identity(&invocation.module)`. If a user switches an invocation to a different generator module or version and leaves the schema and options alone, the cache still hits and the old generator's outputs are kept. The new generator never runs.

findings.summary: Changing an invocation's `output-dir` is not treated as a cache miss, so nothing is generated in the new directory.
findings.detail: `cache_matches` hashes the recorded `entry.outputs` paths, which still point into the old output directory, and never checks them against `invocation.output_dir`. After `output-dir` changes, the old files still exist, so the cache hits. The prior entry with the old paths is kept and the new directory stays empty, so code that imports from the new location fails. The old files are never cleaned up either.

findings.summary: When one invocation's output directory sits inside another's, reconciling the outer directory deletes the inner invocation's freshly generated files.
findings.detail: `kept_by_dir` holds one kept list per output directory. `reconcile_outputs` walks each directory recursively and deletes every `#![generated]` file not in that directory's own list. If A uses `gen` and B uses `gen/b`, reconciling `gen` deletes all of B's outputs because they are not in A's kept list. The lockfile still records them, so every run either regenerates them or leaves them missing. Output dirs are also never checked for `..` or emptiness. `output-dir = "."` normalizes to an empty string, so the whole project root is walked and every `#![generated]` file outside this run's outputs is deleted, including other generators' outputs.

findings.summary: A missing file is reported to the generator as `io` instead of `not-found`, because the CLI host never returns `SourceError::NotFound`.
findings.detail: `read_file` maps only `SourceError::NotFound` to `HostError::NotFound`. `wado_lsp::FilesystemCompilerHost::load_source` turns every `std::fs::read` failure, including ENOENT, into `SourceError::IoError`. A generator that probes optional include paths and handles `not-found` will see `io(...)` instead and may fail with an error. Permission errors are also never reported as `permission-denied`.

findings.summary: Diagnostics a generator emits are dropped when the call traps or runs out of fuel.
findings.detail: Buffered diagnostics are only passed to the host after `call_generate(...).await` succeeds. The `?` on the `map_err` returns early on a trap, fuel exhaustion or another host error. In those cases every diagnostic the generator emitted, which is usually the explanation of what went wrong, is thrown away without being shown.

findings.summary: `validate_module_spec` ignores the version in `module = "ns:name@ver"`, so a version outside the `[build-dependencies]` requirement is accepted.
findings.detail: The lookup compares only `package == ns_name`. The `version` parsed from the spec is checked for emptiness and then discarded. With `proto = { package = "ns:proto", version = "^1.0.0" }`, `module = "ns:proto@9.9.9"` passes validation without a diagnostic, although it cannot resolve against the declared build dependency.

grade.reason: No finding covers walk_and_delete failing on NotFound errors when files or directories are removed concurrently; finding 3 is about nested output dirs deleting each other's files, which is a different defect.

findings.summary: The cache check ignores the generator identity, so changing the generator module or version keeps reusing stale cached outputs.
findings.detail: `cache_matches` compares the primary file, the declared inputs, the reads and the output hashes, and `run_pipeline` also checks `options_hash`. Nothing compares `entry.generator` with `generator_identity(&invocation.module)`. If a user changes `module = "ns:proto@1.0.0"` to `@2.0.0` (or to another generator) and leaves the schema alone, the old entry is still a cache hit. The new generator never runs, the old outputs stay on disk, and the lockfile keeps the old `generator` string.

findings.summary: The cache check ignores a change to `output-dir`, so the new directory stays empty and the files in the old directory are never cleaned up.
findings.detail: `cache_matches` only checks that the recorded output paths still exist with matching hashes. It never checks that they sit under the invocation's current `output_dir`. After `output-dir` changes, the files from the old run still exist, so the entry is a hit and the generator is skipped. `reconcile_outputs` is then run on the new directory, while the kept paths still point into the old one. Consumers that resolve against the new directory find no generated files, and the old files are never deleted.

findings.summary: Output-directory cleanup deletes other invocations' generated files when one output directory contains another, and it can reach outside the project.
findings.detail: `run_pipeline` builds a separate kept list for each `output_dir`, and `walk_and_delete` recurses into every subdirectory. Say invocation A writes to `gen` and B writes to `gen/b`. Cleaning `gen` walks into `gen/b`, sees B's files carry `#![generated]` and are not in A's kept list, and deletes them, so B's outputs are destroyed on every run. An `output-dir` that normalizes to an empty string (e.g. `"/"` or `"."`) makes the walk cover the whole project. A path like `"../x"` is never rejected, so outputs can be written, and generated-marked files deleted, outside the manifest root.

findings.summary: The generator's `read-file` import is not confined to the project, so a sandboxed generator can read any file on disk.
findings.detail: `read_file` passes the path from the guest straight to `host.load_source`. For the CLI that is `wado_lsp::FilesystemCompilerHost::load_source`, which does `base_path.join(path)`. An absolute path replaces the base entirely, and `..` segments climb out of it. A third-party generator from `[build-dependencies]` can therefore read `/etc/passwd`, `~/.ssh/id_rsa` and similar files and put their contents into generated source. This defeats the sandboxing the module docs promise, where only `read-file` and `emit-diagnostic` are linked so generators cannot reach the host.

findings.summary: Generator diagnostics are sent to the inner LSP host rather than the CLI host, so they are never printed.
findings.detail: `run_generator` passes `self.inner.clone()`, the inner `wado_lsp::FilesystemCompilerHost`, as the host for `kiln_runtime::run_generator`. `relay_diagnostic` then calls `emit_diagnostic` on that inner host, which only stores the diagnostic. The CLI wrapper's `emit_diagnostic`, which prints to stderr according to the log level, is skipped. Errors and warnings that a generator reports through `host::emit-diagnostic` are never shown to the user.

findings.summary: `read-file` never returns `not-found` for a missing file, because the CLI host reports every failure as `IoError`.
findings.detail: `read_file` maps `SourceError::NotFound` to `HostError::NotFound` and everything else to `HostError::Io`. The real host, `wado_lsp::FilesystemCompilerHost::load_source`, wraps every `std::fs::read` failure, including ENOENT, in `SourceError::IoError`. A generator that probes for an optional include file and expects `not-found` receives `io("No such file...")`. It will likely treat that as a hard failure, so generators that rely on the WIT contract break.

grade.reason: No finding addresses walk_and_delete aborting with a NotFound error when files or directories are removed concurrently; finding 2 is about nested output dirs deleting other invocations' files, which is a different issue.

entries.defect: The op-only walker (gen_repeat_body) emitted every greedy/non-greedy Optional as a plain one-token first-set check, so it ignored the lowered strategy (lookahead, scan guard, shape lookahead, `??` ATN). Optionals inside LR-suffix bodies were therefore mis-decided.

findings.summary: The save-and-rewind alternative tries (`let saved = p.pos; … if let Err(_) = r_N { p.pos = saved; }`) reset the cursor but leave the `TreeBuilder` as it was, so a failed alternative's tokens and subtrees stay in the tree.
findings.detail: In `gen_multi_alt_body` (around lines 5692-5770), when an alternative is tried speculatively and fails, only `p.pos` is reset; nothing records `p.b.checkpoint()` before the try or calls `p.b.truncate()` after it. Because every `expect`/`match_*` call and every rule wrapper now appends events to the builder, the half-built subtree of the failed alternative stays in the event stream. The next alternative then succeeds and appends its own subtree. The result is a tree with duplicated or extra tokens and nodes, reported as a clean parse (no diagnostics) and highlighted twice. The PR does wrap the repeat-recovery re-parse with checkpoint/truncate, but these partial-scan and no-scan alternative tries were missed.

findings.summary: Required overlapping SimpleCst and General groups no longer fail when no alternative matches, so invalid input is accepted without a diagnostic.
findings.detail: `gen_consume_group_store_op` and `gen_general_group_store_op` used to emit `if let None = {opt} { p.fail(...)?; }` after the overlap dispatch loop. Both checks were removed, and the overlap loops are now just `if/else if` chains with no failing else. These functions are reached from `gen_op_storable_group_inner`, which also runs for the mandatory first iteration of a non-scannable `+` repeat (`while _plus_first || …`). For input where no alternative of an overlapping group like `(a b | a c)+` matches, the mandatory iteration now consumes nothing and returns Ok. The parse continues, or ends with an error at the wrong place, instead of reporting the missing group.

findings.summary: In `gen_lr_fn`, a failing atom or suffix returns through `?` before `p.b.finish_node`, so the LR rule's open node is never closed and the partial tree gets the wrong nesting.
findings.detail: The generated LR function runs `p.b.start_node(RK, _start); _parse_X_atom(p)?; p.b.finish_node(...)`, and each suffix branch runs `start_node_at(...)` followed by `gen_ops` (whose leaves use `?`) and then `finish_node`. LR rules get no outer node from the entry wrapper (`!takes_min_prec`), so nothing else closes these nodes when an error propagates. The unmatched `Open` takes the parent wrappers' `Close` events, which shifts every ancestor's boundary. The fail-soft partial tree returned in `ParseResult` then has the wrong structure and spans, which breaks the promise that open nodes are folded on error.

findings.summary: Rule nodes that match no tokens now get reversed spans (`end < start`), because the old `i32::max(start, p.last_end())` clamp was removed.
findings.detail: The rule wrapper emits `p.b.start_node(rk, p.peek_start())` and then `p.b.finish_node(p.last_end())`. When a rule matches nothing (all elements optional and absent, e.g. the empty `(sql_stmt)` node), `last_end()` is the end of the previous token, which is before `peek_start()`. `tree_build_node` only raises `end` from child spans, so the node is built as `Span::new(start, end)` with `end < start`. `Span::new` does not validate its arguments. The removed `gen_clamped_span_field` existed to prevent exactly this. Consumers that rely on `CstNode.span` (LSP, highlighting, slicing) get invalid ranges.

findings.summary: Box struct names now use `mangle_type_arg_for_generic`, which adds the module to enum (and newtype) names, but the WIR lookup for `&mut <value type>` still builds the name with `mangle_type_name`, so the boxed type for `&mut Enum` is never found.
findings.detail: `get_or_create_box_type` now registers e.g. `Box<./m/Color>` for an enum inner type. `wir_build/context.rs` (Ref/MutRef arm, around lines 902-917) builds `Box<{mangle_type_name(base_inner)}>`, which gives `Box<Color>` for enums (and `Box<i32>` for a newtype after newtype resolution). The `struct_type_map` lookup misses and silently falls back to `inner_wir`, treating the reference as a plain value. Code elsewhere that builds and reads the registered Box struct then disagrees with the parameter and local types. The likely outcome is a Wasm validation ICE, or `&mut` writes to an enum that are lost. Primitives still work only because both manglers return the same string for them.

findings.summary: When the rule name is not found, `to_string_subtree` searches for kind -1, which equals `K_ERROR`, so it can return an `<error>` region instead of an empty string.
findings.detail: The generated helper starts with `_kind = -1` and keeps it when no entry in `GALE_RULE_NAMES` matches, then calls `result.root.find_child(_kind as NodeKind)`. `K_ERROR` is defined as `-1`, so if the root has an error-region child, that region is rendered instead of the documented empty-string result for a missing rule.

grade.reason: None of the findings say that gen_repeat_body emits Optionals in the op-only walker as plain first-set checks and ignores the lowered lookahead, scan-guard, shape-lookahead or `??` strategy.

findings.summary: When a speculative multi-alt parse fails, the parser rewinds `p.pos = saved` but does not roll back the `TreeBuilder`, so the failed alternative's tokens and nodes stay in the CST.
findings.detail: `gen_multi_alt` still emits the save-and-rewind pattern (`let saved = p.pos; let r_i = _alt_i(p); if let Err(_) = r_i { p.pos = saved; }`) for partial-scan, no-scan and fallback alternatives. The rule bodies now append straight to `p.b` (Open/Tok/Close events). On a failed attempt, only the cursor is restored. Every token and sub-node the failed alternative recorded, plus any unclosed `Open` events, stays in the event stream. The next alternative then appends after them. Any grammar that reaches these paths and has an alternative fail part-way produces a clean parse (no diagnostics) with a corrupted tree: duplicated terminals, stray nodes and broken nesting. The repeat-recovery path in this PR uses `checkpoint()`/`truncate()`; these speculative alt paths need the same bracketing.

findings.summary: Required overlapping SimpleCst/General groups no longer fail when no alternative matches, so input that should be rejected can parse silently.
findings.detail: `gen_consume_group_store_op` and `gen_general_group_store_op` used to emit `if let None = opt { p.fail(...)?; }` after the overlap dispatch. That check was removed, and the dispatch chains (`gen_simplecst_overlap_loop`, `gen_general_overlap_loop`) have no `else` arm. These ops are the body of storable `+` repeats, and their first iteration runs unconditionally (`_plus_first` loops). If the lookahead fits none of the overlapping alternatives, that first iteration consumes nothing and reports nothing. The loop then exits, so `(a b | a c)+` accepts zero iterations. The mandatory element is skipped without a diagnostic, or the error is reported later at the wrong token. The code comment assumes a repeat guard always checked first, but that does not hold for the first `+` iteration.

findings.summary: Box struct names now use the module-qualified mangler, but `wir_build/context.rs` still looks up `Box<T>` by the unqualified `mangle_type_name`, so lookups for enum-typed `&T`/`&mut T` miss.
findings.detail: `TypeBuilder` now registers boxes as `Box<{mangle_type_arg_for_generic(inner)}>`, which for `Enum` (and other named value types) yields `Box<module/Color>`. `type_id_to_wir_type` for `ResolvedType::Ref`/`MutRef` over a value type still builds `mangle_generic_name("Box", [type_table.mangle_type_name(base_inner)])`, i.e. `Box<Color>`. It then looks that name up in `struct_type_map`. The lookup fails and falls back to the unboxed value type (`inner_wir`). A `&mut` of an enum then lowers to a plain i32 in some places and a Box ref in others, which can cause WIR type mismatches or lose the mutable-location semantics. Primitives are unaffected only because both manglers agree on them.

findings.summary: On a parse error, left-recursive rules leave unclosed CST nodes, so the partial tree returned for broken input has the wrong nesting.
findings.detail: `gen_lr_fn` emits `p.b.start_node(RK, _start); _parse_X_atom(p)?; p.b.finish_node(...)`. Suffix branches emit `p.b.start_node_at(_cp, ...)` followed by `gen_ops` leaves that use `?`. When the atom or a suffix element fails, the `?` returns before `finish_node`, leaving an `Open` with no matching `Close`. The LR wrapper deliberately opens no node of its own, so nothing closes it. Each enclosing non-LR wrapper's `finish_node` then closes the wrong (innermost) node. The resulting `ParseResult.root` for broken input has misplaced siblings and spans. This contradicts the stated fail-soft guarantee that open nodes are folded closed as the error propagates.

findings.summary: `expect`/`match_set` on `TK_EOF` append the EOF token without advancing, so a grammar that references EOF more than once gets the same token in the tree several times.
findings.detail: The new `self.b.token(self.pos); return Ok(self.pos);` in the EOF branch records the EOF index on every match. With `prog : x EOF EOF` (the multiple_eof fixture) the tree gets two `Token(eof)` children with the same index. `highlight_walk` visits each one, and `hl_visit_token` emits the token's trivia captures again on each visit. Trailing comments or whitespace before EOF are therefore highlighted twice, producing duplicate or overlapping spans in the HTML output.

findings.summary: The `RK_<UPPER>` node-kind constants collide for parser rules whose names differ only in letter case, so the generated module fails to compile.
findings.detail: `gen_node_kinds` (and `rule_kind_const` in parser_gen) build the constant name by uppercasing the whole rule name. Parser rules `fooBar` and `foobar` (both legal ANTLR parser-rule names) both become `global RK_FOOBAR`, a duplicate global definition. The previous typed path used each rule's own type name and did not have this collision.

grade.reason: None of the findings say that the op-only walker emits Optionals inside LR-suffix bodies as plain first-set checks and ignores the lowered strategy (lookahead, scan guard, shape lookahead, or the `??` ATN).

findings.summary: Speculative multi-alt parses rewind `p.pos` on failure but never roll back the `TreeBuilder`, so the failed alternative's tokens and nodes stay in the final CST.
findings.detail: In `gen_parse_fn_named`'s Ambiguous fallback (both the partial-scan path and the no-scan save/rewind path around lines 5692–5771), a failed `_alt_N` is undone with only `p.pos = saved;`. Under the new emitter every `expect`/`match_*` and every rule wrapper writes events into `p.b`. Rewinding the cursor therefore leaves the failed attempt's `Tok`/`Open`/`Close` events behind. The next alternative then re-appends the same tokens. A parse that succeeds with no diagnostics still returns a tree with duplicated terminals and stray subtrees. The PR adds a `checkpoint()`/`truncate()` bracket for the recovery re-parse in `gen_rep_break_with_recovery`, but not at these backtracking sites.

findings.summary: Overlapping SimpleCst/General group dispatch no longer fails when no alternative matches, so the mandatory first iteration of `(...)+` can match nothing without any error.
findings.detail: `gen_consume_group_store_op` / `gen_general_group_store_op` used to end the overlap path with `if let None = opt { p.fail(...)?; }`. That check was removed, and `gen_simplecst_overlap_loop` / `gen_general_overlap_loop` emit an `if/else if` chain with no `else`. For a `+` repeat, the first iteration runs unconditionally (`while _plus_first || ...`, or the scannable `loop` with `_plus_first`). When the lookahead is in none of the groups' first sets, nothing is consumed and no error is raised; the loop then exits. A required one-or-more group is accepted as zero matches. The parse either succeeds on invalid input or reports the error later at a misleading position.

findings.summary: Node-kind constants are named by uppercasing the rule name, so rules that differ only in letter case (e.g. `fooBar` and `foobar`) both emit `global RK_FOOBAR` and the generated parser does not compile.
findings.detail: `gen_node_kinds` emits `RK_{rule_const(name)}` and `rule_kind_const` in parser_gen.wado uses the same scheme, where `rule_const` is `to_ascii_uppercase`. ANTLR rule names are case-sensitive, so two distinct parser rules can map to the same identifier. The result is a duplicate global definition, and the wrappers' `start_node(RK_..)` calls become ambiguous. Grammars of this kind generated fine before this change.

grade.reason: None of the findings concern the op-only walker's Optional emission ignoring the lowered strategy (lookahead, scan guard, shape lookahead, non-greedy ATN). They cover TreeBuilder rollback, missing group-dispatch failure, and RK_ constant name collisions.

entries.defect: For path-form method calls like `Scale::scaled(&p, 2, 3)`, the receiver is passed as `args[0]`, but self params were filtered from the parameter-name list, so every label shifted one argument left (`factor:` on `&p`, `bias:` on `2`).

findings.summary: Type hints are emitted even when the recorded type is `Unknown` or `Error`, so the editor shows inlay hints like `: unknown` or `: error`.
findings.detail: `push_type_hint` turns any `TypeId` recorded through `record_local_symbol` into a label using `TypeTable::type_name`, and it never checks for `ResolvedType::Unknown` or `ResolvedType::Error`. Several elaborator paths record exactly those types. `closure_param_type` returns `TypeTable::UNKNOWN` for an unannotated closure parameter when there is no expected function type (for example `let g = |x| x + 1;`, the case covered by `closure_param_type_without_annotation_emits_type_hint`, whose loose assertion would also pass on `: unknown`). Destructured for-of elements use `unwrap_or(TypeTable::UNKNOWN)`. A let whose initializer has a type error records the error type. In each case the user sees a misleading `: unknown` or `: error` annotation in their source instead of no hint. The fix is to skip hints whose type resolves to `Unknown` or `Error`.

grade.reason: The only finding is about type hints showing `: unknown`/`: error`; it never mentions path-form method calls whose parameter-name hints shift because the self param was filtered out.

findings.summary: Type hints are emitted even when the elaborator recorded an `Unknown`/`Error` type, so the editor shows `: unknown` or `: error` labels on bindings it could not infer.
findings.detail: `record_local_symbol` now stores the binding's `TypeId` in `local_types` for every binding. That includes bindings whose type fell back to `TypeTable::UNKNOWN`: for example `let x = undefined_fn();`, a tuple element that is out of range in `resolve_variadic_for_of` (`unwrap_or(TypeTable::UNKNOWN)`), or a closure parameter with no expected type. `Semantics::local_type_name` sends the id to `TypeTable::type_name`, which returns "unknown" for `Unknown` and "error" for `Error`. `push_type_hint` never checks for these cases, so the editor shows inlay text that is not a real type and makes invalid code look annotated. Code with errors is exactly what the LSP sees while the user is typing, and the PR says it supports partial results.

findings.summary: Struct-destructuring shorthand gets a type hint placed right after the field name, so `let { x, y } = p` renders as `let { x: i32, y: i32 } = p`, which reads as the rename syntax `field: pattern`.
findings.detail: `hint_pattern_bindings` recurses into `Pattern::Struct` fields and anchors a `: T` hint at the end of each leaf `Ident` span. For the shorthand `{ x }` the leaf span is the field name itself. The rendered text `{ x: i32 }` is the same as the struct-pattern form that binds field `x` to a sub-pattern named `i32`, so the hint misstates what the code does rather than just showing its type. The new test `struct_destructure_let_hints_each_field_binding` locks this behaviour in.

grade.reason: Neither finding covers self params being filtered out of path-form static method calls, which shifts the parameter labels by one argument; the findings are about unknown/error type hints and struct shorthand hint rendering.

findings.summary: When the elaborator could not infer a binding's type, the type hint still renders the placeholder as text, so users see `: unknown` or `: error`.
findings.detail: `push_type_hint` emits a hint whenever `Semantics::local_type_name` returns a value, and that value is just `TypeTable::type_name(type_id)`. The PR records whatever `TypeId` the elaborator had at `record_local_symbol` time, and that is often a placeholder. `closure_param_type` returns `TypeTable::UNKNOWN` for an unannotated closure parameter with no expected function type (e.g. `let g = |x| x + 1;`). The destructuring path in stmt.rs records `inner_elems.get(i).unwrap_or(TypeTable::UNKNOWN)`. An unannotated `let` whose initializer failed to type-check takes the value's `UNKNOWN`/`Error` type. `type_name` renders these as `unknown` and `error`, so the editor shows hints like `x: unknown` or `y: error`. Those labels are wrong and are not valid Wado type syntax. This happens all the time while a user is typing in a partially broken file. The test `closure_param_without_annotation_emits_type_hint` does not catch it: it accepts any type hint on that line, and the `let g` hint already satisfies it. Placeholder types (Unknown/Error, and arguably types that contain them) should be skipped instead of shown.

grade.reason: The only finding is about placeholder type names showing up in type hints. It says nothing about self params being filtered out of path-form method calls, which shifts the parameter-name labels one slot.

entries.defect: The block parser let any list marker (e.g. a wrapped `2010) b` line), a link reference definition, or any HTML-tag-like line interrupt an open paragraph, and blockquotes had no lazy continuation, so the formatter rewrote paragraph text into lists, ref defs, or HTML blocks.

findings.summary: `render` panics when a link reference definition appears inside a list item.
findings.detail: `render_blocks` skips `LinkReferenceDef` nodes, but list items render through `render_item_children` → `render_item_child` → `render_block`. `render_block` has no arm for `LinkReferenceDef`, so it hits `_ => panic("unexpected node in block position")`. `parse_blocks` emits that node for any item line such as `- [a]: /url` (or an indented definition under an item), so ordinary user input crashes the renderer.

findings.summary: Emphasis whose opening `*` follows a letter or digit is rewritten to `_`, which GitHub does not treat as emphasis inside a word.
findings.detail: `keep_asterisk` only checks the character after the closing delimiter (`next_is_alnum`). For `foo*bar*`, the opener sits mid-word but the closer is at the end, so `keep_asterisk` is false and the printer outputs `foo_bar_`. That re-parses as literal text, so formatting silently drops the emphasis and the output renders differently.

findings.summary: A code span whose content contains a run of two or more backticks is printed with a `` `` `` delimiter that clashes with that content.
findings.detail: `print_code_span` uses two backticks whenever the content contains any backtick, without looking at the longest run. Content such as ``a``b`` (from a source span written with three-backtick delimiters) is printed as ``` ``a``b`` ```. That re-parses as a different code span plus literal text, so formatting corrupts the document.

findings.summary: An HTML tag at the start of a paragraph's continuation line wrongly ends the paragraph and starts a raw HTML block.
findings.detail: `parse_blocks` checks `is_html_block_start` before it appends a line to the open paragraph, and it ignores `para`. CommonMark type-7 HTML blocks cannot interrupt a paragraph. So `Press\n<kbd>C</kbd> to copy` becomes a paragraph plus an Html block that swallows every following line up to the next blank line. The formatter then inserts a blank line, splitting the paragraph, and `render` emits the swallowed Markdown as escaped literal text.

findings.summary: A nested list that follows a blank line inside a list item is pulled out of the item, so formatting moves it to the top level.
findings.detail:
In `parse_list`, a line after a blank line continues the item only if `parse_list_marker(...)` is `None`. So `- a

  - nested` ends the outer list at the blank line, and `  - nested` is parsed as a separate top-level list. The printer outputs `- a

- nested`, which re-parses as one loose list with two sibling items. The nesting is lost.

findings.summary: A shortcut reference link is printed from its normalized child text instead of its raw label, so the label can stop matching its definition.
findings.detail: `print_shortcut_link` prints `print_inline_seq(&link.children)` and never uses `link.label`. If the link text contains emphasis written with `*` (e.g. `[*foo*]` with `[*foo*]: /x`), the printer outputs `[_foo_]`. Its normalized label `_foo_` no longer matches the definition `*foo*`, so the link turns into literal text after formatting.

findings.summary: A closure with an explicit `-> Type` annotation skips the missing-return and body/return-type mismatch diagnostics.
findings.detail: When `declared_return` is `Some`, `return_type` is set straight to the declared type, bypassing the `ast_block_always_exits` / `MissingReturn` checks that block-bodied closures otherwise get. `|x: i32| -> i32 { if x > 0 { return 1; } }` falls off the end with a unit tail but is accepted without a diagnostic. It then lowers to a function declared to return i32 whose body can end with no value, producing invalid code instead of a compile error.

findings.summary: Setext headings are not recognized, so formatting turns a `Title\n---` heading into a paragraph followed by a thematic break.
findings.detail:
`parse_blocks` checks `is_thematic_break` before adding a line to the open paragraph and has no setext handling. `Title ---` (an h2 in CommonMark/GFM) is parsed as Paragraph + ThematicBreak, and the printer outputs `Title ---`. The heading is permanently rewritten as a paragraph and a horizontal rule, and `render` emits `

`/`

` instead of `

`.

findings.summary: Adjacent lists that differ only in bullet character (or ordered delimiter) are printed with the same marker and merge into one list on re-parse.
findings.detail:
`parse_list` splits `- a
* b` into two lists because `base_delim` differs. `print_list` normalizes every bullet to `-` and every ordered delimiter to `.`, so the output `- a

- b` re-parses as a single loose list. Formatting changes the document's structure; the old renderer even had a test that such lists render as two separate `<ul>`s.

grade.reason: Finding 3 says a type-7 HTML-tag-like line wrongly interrupts an open paragraph in `parse_blocks`, which is one of the paragraph-interruption bugs the fix addresses.

findings.summary: `render` panics when a list item contains a link reference definition, for example `- [a]: /url`.
findings.detail: Inside a list item, `parse_list` hands the item's lines to `parse_blocks`, and `try_ref_def_line` turns `[a]: /url` into a `Node::LinkReferenceDef` child of the item. `render_item_child` sends every non-paragraph child to `render_block`. `render_block` has no arm for `LinkReferenceDef`, so it reaches `_ => panic("marl-html: unexpected node in block position")`. Only `render_blocks`, which handles the document and blockquote levels, skips definitions; list items never go through it. Any Markdown file with a reference definition inside a list item therefore crashes the renderer.

findings.summary: Emphasis written with asterisks right after a letter or digit (`foo*bar*`) is printed as `foo_bar_`, which is no longer emphasis.
findings.detail: `resolve_pair` sets `keep_asterisk` only from `closer.next_is_alnum`, the character after the closing run. It never looks at the character before the opening run. For `foo*bar*` the closer is followed by end of input, so `keep_asterisk` is false and `print_emphasis` writes `_`. Underscores inside a word cannot open or close emphasis, so the formatted text re-parses as the literal `foo_bar_`. The formatter changes what the document means.

findings.summary: Link and definition destinations written in angle brackets lose their brackets when printed, so a URL with a space is cut short.
findings.detail: `parse_dest_and_title` removes the `<...>` around a destination such as `<a b>`, and the AST does not record that brackets were there. `print_dest_and_title` and `print_link_ref_def` then write the bare URL. `[x](<a b>)` becomes `[x](a b)`. On re-parse the destination is just `a`, and `b` is not a valid title, so it is dropped. The same happens to `[r]: <url with spaces>`. The URL is silently corrupted.

findings.summary: Hard line breaks made with two trailing spaces are dropped, so `format` turns them into soft breaks.
findings.detail:
In the space/tab branch of `tokenize`, a run of spaces right before ` ` counts as `at_end` and is thrown away; only a backslash before the newline produces `Node::HardBreak`. For `a b` the parser produces Text, SoftBreak, Text, and the printer writes `a b`. GFM renders the original with a `
`, so formatting removes the line break the author wrote.

findings.summary: Setext headings are not recognised: a `---` underline becomes a thematic break, and formatting turns the heading into a paragraph followed by a rule.
findings.detail: `parse_blocks` checks `is_thematic_break` before adding a line to the open paragraph, and it has no setext-heading handling at all. `Title\n---` is parsed as Paragraph("Title") plus ThematicBreak. `print_block_sequence` then puts a blank line between them, so the formatted file no longer contains the `<h2>` heading. `Title\n===` stays a plain paragraph.

findings.summary: The formatter keeps only the first word of a fenced code block's info string and drops the rest.
findings.detail: `parse_fenced_code` stores just `first_word(info)` as `CodeBlock.tag`, and `print_code_block` writes only that tag. A fence like ```` ```js {1,3} ```` or ```` ```rust title="x" ```` loses its extra attributes every time `format` runs, which other tools may depend on. The `fmt_ast.wado` doc comment says the AST keeps enough of the source to round-trip, but this part is lost.

findings.summary: A code span whose content contains two backticks in a row is printed with double-backtick delimiters, which breaks the span.
findings.detail: `print_code_span` uses ``` `` ``` whenever the content contains any backtick, whatever the longest backtick run is. For content `a``b` (written in the source as ```` ```a``b``` ````) it prints ``` ``a``b`` ```. On re-parse the span closes at the inner ``` `` ```, so the code text and the surrounding text change. The delimiter has to be longer than the longest backtick run in the content, as `fence_string` already does for fenced code.

findings.summary: Two adjacent lists with different bullet markers or delimiters are merged into one loose list by the formatter.
findings.detail: The parser starts a new list when the marker changes (for example `- a` then `* b`, or `1.` then `1)`), giving two `List` nodes. The printer writes every unordered marker as `-` and every ordered delimiter as `.`, with a blank line between the two blocks. The result re-parses as a single loose list, so list structure and HTML output change.

findings.summary: When a closure has an explicit `-> T` return type, the missing-return check is skipped completely.
findings.detail: With `declared_return` set, `return_type` becomes `dt` right away. The `ast_find_return_type_in_block` / `ast_block_always_exits` checks that report `TypeError::MissingReturn` never run. A closure like `|x: i32| -> i32 { if x > 0 { return 1; } }` has a unit-typed body that can fall off the end, yet it is accepted with type `fn(i32) -> i32`. That can produce invalid Wasm or wrong behaviour where the compiler should have reported an error.

grade.reason: No finding addresses paragraph interruption by list markers, link reference definitions, or HTML lines, nor the missing blockquote lazy continuation; the setext finding concerns a different paragraph-interruption issue.

findings.summary: `render` panics when a link reference definition sits inside a list item.
findings.detail: `render_item_children` hands every non-paragraph child to `render_block`, and `render_block` has no arm for `Node::LinkReferenceDef`, so it falls through to `panic("marl-html: unexpected node in block position")`. Only `render_blocks` skips these nodes, and list items never go through it. `parse_blocks` emits a `LinkReferenceDef` node for any `[x]: url` line in an item, so input like `- [a]: /x` crashes the HTML renderer.

findings.summary: Emphasis is rewritten to `_..._` even when the opening `*` follows a letter or digit, which turns the emphasis into literal text.
findings.detail: `keep_asterisk` only looks at the character after the closing delimiter (`closer.next_is_alnum`). For `foo*bar* baz` the opener follows `o`, so the printer writes `foo_bar_ baz`. An underscore inside a word cannot open emphasis, so after formatting the emphasis is gone and the asterisks are lost.

findings.summary: `print_code_span` never uses more than two backticks, so code that contains a double-backtick run breaks the span.
findings.detail: For content like ``a``b`` (parsed from three-backtick delimiters) the printer writes it between pairs of backticks. On re-parse the inner double-backtick run closes the span early, so the formatter changes the document. The delimiter needs to be longer than the longest backtick run in the content, as `fence_string` already does for code blocks.

findings.summary: Link destinations and titles are printed without their original quoting, so spaces, angle brackets and quotes corrupt the link.
findings.detail: `parse_dest_and_title` strips the `<...>` around a destination, and `print_dest_and_title` / `print_link_ref_def` print the URL bare with the title always in double quotes. `[a](<x y>)` becomes `[a](x y)`, which re-parses with URL `x` and the `y` thrown away. A title like `'say "hi"'` becomes `"say "hi""`, which cuts the title short.

findings.summary: Hard line breaks made with two trailing spaces are silently removed by the formatter.
findings.detail: The whitespace branch of `tokenize` drops every space or tab run before a newline and emits a soft break, so `a  \nb` (a CommonMark/GitHub hard break) formats to `a\nb`. This changes how the document renders, and running `marl format` writes the change to disk.

findings.summary: A paragraph line that starts with an inline HTML tag is treated as an HTML block that interrupts the paragraph, and the formatter then inserts a blank line.
findings.detail: `parse_blocks` runs `is_html_block_start` without checking for an open paragraph, and it accepts any tag even when more text follows on the line. In CommonMark, an HTML block of type 7 cannot interrupt a paragraph. So `text bold more` is split, and `print_block_sequence` writes `text bold more`, turning one paragraph into two blocks.

findings.summary: Setext headings are not recognised, so the formatter turns them into a paragraph followed by a horizontal rule.
findings.detail:
In `Title
---`, `is_thematic_break` matches the underline, which ends the paragraph and emits a `ThematicBreak`. The printer then writes `Title

---`, so an h2 heading becomes a paragraph plus a horizontal rule. (`===` underlines stay as paragraph text.) Running the formatter changes the document's meaning.

findings.summary: Lazy continuation lines in blockquotes are not supported, so the formatter moves text out of the quote.
findings.detail:
`parse_blockquote` stops at the first line that does not start with `>`. For `> a
b`, CommonMark makes `b` part of the quoted paragraph, but here it becomes a separate paragraph. The printer then always puts a blank line after a BlockQuote, giving `> a

b`, which moves the text out of the quote.

findings.summary: An explicit closure return-type annotation turns off the missing-return diagnostic.
findings.detail: When `declared_return` is set, `return_type` is just the declared type, and the `ast_block_always_exits` / `MissingReturn` check is skipped. A closure like `|x: i32| -> i32 { if x > 0 { return 1; } }` or `|| -> i32 {}` gets no diagnostic even though its body can finish with unit. This leads to a type mismatch or invalid Wasm instead of a compile error.

grade.reason: The known defect explicitly includes the missing lazy continuation in blockquotes, which the fix addresses in `parse_blockquote`, and finding 7 describes exactly that bug and its effect of moving text out of the quote.
